event.text:
Phase 1 -- system map: document the analyzed service's components, external
dependencies, and entry points as SystemComponent entries (kind: service, worker, job,
external-dependency, datastore, or entrypoint), each with a stable ID and a
description; record dependencies between components via `depends_on`. Propose every
entry through the `propose_edits` tool, tagged for phase 1 -- free-form text never
changes the artifacts.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
I'll start by loading the tool schemas and exploring the codebase.
Source read. This is a small key-value service: one public read path (`get_value`), an in-memory cache, a flat-file store, a background evictor, and an internal write path. Proposing the phase 1 map.

payload_or_id.name: get_value read entrypoint
payload_or_id.description: kvstore/api.py:get_value(cache, key) -- the only client-facing operation the service exposes. Delegates the read to Cache.get, catches StorageError to increment the request counter with outcome="error" and re-raises, otherwise increments outcome="success" and returns the value. This is the sole point of instrumentation in the whole package: it emits kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}. It cannot distinguish a correct value from a stale or wrong one, because a cache hit returns whatever the cache holds and never reaches storage.

payload_or_id.name: In-memory cache layer
payload_or_id.description: kvstore/cache.py:Cache -- an unbounded in-process dict of key -> Entry(value, inserted_at_ms) sitting in front of Storage. get() returns a cached entry if the key is present and otherwise reads through to Storage and caches the result (including a None miss). It has no expiry logic of its own: entries live until something calls evict(key). It exposes items() so the evictor can walk entries and evict(key) so the evictor -- or a writer -- can remove one. No metric is emitted here, so hit/miss ratio, entry count, and read-through volume are all invisible.

payload_or_id.name: Flat-file key-value storage
payload_or_id.description: kvstore/storage.py:Storage -- persists all keys to a single delimited text file at a configured Path, one "key,value" line per pair. get() returns None if the file is absent, otherwise linearly scans every line and partitions on the first comma. put() reads the whole file into a dict, sets the key, creates the parent directory, and rewrites the entire file. Both wrap OSError in StorageError. The whole-file rewrite is non-atomic, the scan is O(file size) per read, and the comma-delimited, unescaped format means a key or value containing a comma or newline is not round-tripped faithfully. Emits no metrics: latency, file size, and read/write errors are only visible downstream at the entrypoint, and only for reads.

payload_or_id.name: Background cache eviction pass
payload_or_id.description: kvstore/evictor.py:run_eviction_pass(cache) -- the only mechanism that bounds cache growth. Walks Cache.items(), collects keys whose age exceeds TTL_SECONDS (300s), evicts them, and returns the count so a caller can observe progress. The scheduler loop that invokes it periodically is not part of this repo, so how often it runs -- or whether it runs at all -- is unobservable from here. The comparison is unit-mismatched: `now` is epoch seconds while Entry.inserted_at_ms is epoch milliseconds, so `now - inserted_at_ms` is always a large negative number, the expiry condition is never true, and the pass evicts nothing. Its return value, the one signal it produces, is not recorded as a metric.

payload_or_id.name: Internal write path (update_value)
payload_or_id.description: kvstore/admin.py:update_value(storage, cache, key, value) -- internal, non-client-facing write path. Calls Storage.put(key, value) only. It receives the Cache as a parameter but never calls cache.evict(key), so a key already resident in the cache keeps serving the pre-write value indefinitely (the evictor that would eventually expire it does not work). Not reachable from external clients and entirely uninstrumented: write volume, write errors, and write latency produce no signal anywhere.

payload_or_id.name: Periodic data-sync job (caller of the write path)
payload_or_id.description: The periodic job that drives kvstore/admin.py:update_value, named in that module's docstring as the intended caller. Its code is outside this repo, so its schedule, batch size, and success/failure are not observable from the service. It is the only producer of writes, which makes it the upstream origin of every staleness chain that ends in a client reading an outdated value from the cache.

payload_or_id.name: Local filesystem hosting the store file
payload_or_id.description: The filesystem holding the Storage path and its parent directory. Reads depend on the file being present and readable; writes depend on the parent directory being creatable and the volume having free space and inodes. Every failure of this dependency surfaces as an OSError that Storage converts to StorageError, which is visible only on the read path via the entrypoint's error-labeled counter -- write-side failures reach no instrumentation at all.

payload_or_id.name: prometheus_client registry and scrape path
payload_or_id.description: prometheus_client 0.26.0 (requirements.txt) provides the Counter used by api.py and the default registry holding it. This repo defines the metric but never starts an HTTP exposition endpoint or pushes to a gateway, so nothing in the code confirms the counter is reachable by a Prometheus server. Every alert recommended by this analysis depends on this scrape path working; if it is unwired or unscraped, the metrics go to a black hole and alerts silently never fire.

event.text:
Phase 1 accepted. Eight components proposed. **System map** ```mermaid graph TD DS[sm-job-data-sync
periodic data-sync job] --> AD[sm-entrypoint-admin-update-value
internal write path] AD --> ST[sm-datastore-flatfile-storage] GV[sm-entrypoint-get-value
public read API] --> CA[sm-service-cache] GV --> PC[sm-dep-prometheus-client] CA --> ST EV[sm-job-evictor
background eviction] --> CA ST --> FS[sm-dep-filesystem] ``` **Entry points (2)** — `get_value` is the only client-facing operation and the only instrumented code in the package; `update_value` is an internal write path reachable only from the data-sync job. **Structural observations carried forward to phase 2**, each of which is an upstream link rather than a user-visible symptom: - **The write path takes `Cache` as a parameter and never uses it.** `update_value` writes storage only, so a cached key keeps serving the pre-write value. The seam to fix it (`cache.evict`) exists and is uncalled. - **The evictor is the only bound on cache size, and it evicts nothing.** `now` is epoch seconds, `Entry.inserted_at_ms` is epoch milliseconds, so the age expression is always large and negative and the TTL condition is never true. This makes the staleness above permanent rather than bounded by 300s — the two defects compound. - **The evictor's scheduler is not in this repo.** "Pass returns 0" and "pass never ran" are indistinguishable from outside, and the return count it computes for exactly this purpose is discarded rather than recorded. - **Instrumentation stops at the entrypoint.** Cache hit/miss, entry count, storage latency, storage file size, and the entire write path emit nothing. A cache hit never reaches storage, so the one existing counter cannot tell a correct value from a stale one. - **`sm-dep-prometheus-client` is listed as a dependency deliberately.** The `Counter` is defined but nothing in the repo starts an exposition endpoint or push. Every alert this run recommends rests on a scrape path no code here confirms exists — I'll treat wiring that as a prerequisite in phase 4 rather than assuming it. Two storage-level issues I noted in the component description and will decide on in phase 2: the non-atomic whole-file rewrite in `put()`, and the unescaped comma/newline delimiting that silently fails to round-trip keys or values containing either. Ready for phase 2 when you are.

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
Enumerating failure chains from the user-visible ends backwards to root causes.

payload_or_id.name: Client reads a permanently stale value after a write
payload_or_id.description: get_value returns a value that was correct before the last write and is now wrong, and keeps returning it for the life of the process. Cache.get short-circuits on any resident key and never re-consults storage, so once a key is cached the only ways it can ever change are eviction or a restart. Neither happens: the write path does not invalidate, and the evictor's TTL check can never fire. The service reports outcome="success" for every one of these reads.

payload_or_id.name: Client reads None forever for a key that does exist in storage
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get caches the result of a miss, storing Entry(value=None) for keys absent from storage. If a key is read before the data-sync job writes it, the None is cached and served indefinitely afterwards -- the later write to storage cannot dislodge it. This is a distinct outcome from stale-value staleness because the key never had a correct cached value to go stale: a single premature read permanently hides a key from every client. Indistinguishable at the entrypoint from a legitimately absent key, since both return None with outcome="success".

payload_or_id.name: Process is OOM-killed, taking the service down
payload_or_id.description: The cache holds every key ever requested, so under sustained unique-key traffic resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed by the OOM killer or the container's memory limit. Every in-flight request fails and the service is unavailable until it restarts -- at which point the cache is empty and the climb begins again, giving a sawtooth of periodic outages whose interval depends only on traffic mix. Nothing in the process observes its own memory or entry count, so the first signal is the kill itself.

payload_or_id.name: get_value raises StorageError to the client
payload_or_id.description: A read that misses the cache reaches Storage.get, which converts any OSError into StorageError; api.py increments outcome="error" and re-raises to the caller. This is the one failure mode the service instruments today and the only one alertable without new instrumentation. Note the coupling to cache state: with a warm cache only miss traffic is affected, so a completely unreadable backing file can present as a partial rather than total failure, and its blast radius grows immediately after any restart.

payload_or_id.name: Client reads a corrupted or foreign value from delimiter collision
payload_or_id.description: The store's line format is unescaped "key,value" split on the first comma. A value containing a comma round-trips intact, but a key containing a comma is silently re-partitioned on read: writing key "a,b" with value "x" produces the line "a,b,x", which reads back as key "a" with value "b,x". A value containing a newline is worse -- it writes a spurious extra line that becomes a phantom key/value pair, and can shadow or overwrite a real key on the next put(). The result is a client receiving a well-formed value that belongs to a different key, reported as outcome="success". Silent data corruption with no signal at any layer.

payload_or_id.name: Previously written keys disappear from the store
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put rewrites the entire file from an in-memory dict via a single write_text, with no temp-file-and-rename and no lock. A crash, kill, or ENOSPC partway through leaves the file truncated or partially written, destroying keys that were never touched by the write that failed -- the blast radius of one bad write is the whole dataset. Clients see previously-good keys start returning None, or an unparseable tail. Recovery requires a restore; the service itself neither detects nor reports the loss.

payload_or_id.name: Read latency degrades as the store file grows
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads the entire file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size) and the whole file is allocated per miss. This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after a restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been. There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so this manifests to clients as slow reads with no corresponding signal.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass evicts nothing due to a seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in epoch seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, which cache.py sets to `time.time() * 1000`. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS, so expired_keys is always empty and the pass always returns 0. The single mechanism that bounds cache memory and the single mechanism that eventually corrects a stale entry are the same mechanism, and it is dead. Rated critical despite not being user-visible because it is the shared root of both the OOM chain and the staleness chain, and it is the earliest point at which either can be detected.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass is a plain function; the scheduler loop that should call it periodically lives outside this repo. If that loop is missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged, eviction simply never runs. This is a separate failure from the unit mismatch and produces identical downstream effects, which matters for detection: a pass that returns 0 and a pass that never ran are indistinguishable unless the pass itself emits a signal on every execution. Fixing the unit bug alone leaves this failure entirely undetectable.

payload_or_id.name: Write path does not invalidate the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value takes a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put, never cache.evict(key). The seam needed to fix it already exists and is documented in cache.py as intended for exactly this caller. On its own this would bound staleness to one TTL period; combined with the dead evictor it makes staleness permanent. The unused parameter is the tell -- the invalidation was designed and then not wired.

payload_or_id.name: Cache entry count and footprint grow without bound
payload_or_id.description: Entries are only ever added, never removed, so the dict grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys ever requested. Growth rate is set by the unique-key rate rather than the request rate, which means a scan, a crawler, or a key namespace with high cardinality drives it far faster than normal traffic would suggest. This is the observable precursor to the OOM kill and the point at which the chain can be caught with hours or days of warning instead of none.

payload_or_id.name: Cache has no maximum size or replacement policy
payload_or_id.description: Cache is a bare dict with no capacity limit and no LRU/LFU replacement. There is no backstop if the evictor is broken or stalled: correctness of the memory bound rests entirely on an external background job. A capacity bound would degrade gracefully into extra storage reads rather than into an OOM kill, and would make the eviction job a performance optimisation rather than a load-bearing safety mechanism.

payload_or_id.name: Cache stores negative results indefinitely
payload_or_id.description: On a storage miss, Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) rather than declining to cache. Two consequences: an attacker or a buggy client requesting random non-existent keys inflates the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain; and a key read before it is first written is permanently pinned to None. Negative caching is a legitimate design choice, but only with a TTL, and this cache has no working expiry.

payload_or_id.name: Full cache loss on restart causes a read-through stampede
payload_or_id.description: The cache is process-local with no warming or persistence, so every restart -- including the OOM-kill restarts this design produces -- empties it. Every subsequent request is a miss that reads and scans the whole store file, so storage load and read latency spike hardest exactly when the service is recovering. This couples the OOM chain to the latency chain: each memory-exhaustion crash is followed by the worst-case latency window.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file unreadable (permissions, I/O error, unmounted volume)
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get raises OSError -- and hence StorageError -- if the file exists but cannot be read: permission change, hardware or network-volume I/O error, unmounted path, or exhausted file descriptors. Note the asymmetry deliberately built into get(): a file that does not exist at all returns None rather than raising, so a lost or wrong path presents as every key having silently vanished rather than as an error. That variant is the more dangerous one, because it produces outcome="success" for every read.

payload_or_id.name: Filesystem full or out of inodes on write
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put must materialise the entire dataset as a single string and write it in one call, so it needs free space of the order of the whole file on every single write, and briefly holds the dataset twice in memory. On ENOSPC the write_text fails partway, leaving the file truncated -- the non-atomic rewrite converts a full disk directly into dataset-wide data loss rather than into a rejected write.

payload_or_id.name: put() rewrites the whole file in place without atomic replace
payload_or_id.description: write_text truncates the target and writes in place, with no write-to-temp-and-rename and no fsync. Any interruption between truncation and completion -- crash, OOM kill, deploy, ENOSPC -- leaves a partial file. The window is proportional to the dataset size, so the risk grows as the store grows. It also means a concurrent reader can observe the file mid-rewrite.

payload_or_id.name: Reader observes the file mid-rewrite
payload_or_id.description: With no locking between get() and put(), a read overlapping a rewrite can see a truncated or partially written file. The read then returns None for keys that exist (they were in the not-yet-written tail) or raises StorageError on an I/O failure. Because misses are cached, a None read during this window is captured into the cache and outlives the rewrite that caused it -- a transient storage race is promoted into permanent wrong state.

payload_or_id.name: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: put() is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file. Two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish discards every key the first added. There is no lock, no compare-and-swap, and no version check. Both writers report success. Whether this can fire depends on the deployment -- a single-threaded sync job makes it unreachable -- so it warrants confirming the concurrency model rather than assuming either way.

payload_or_id.name: Unescaped delimiter format does not round-trip keys or values
payload_or_id.description: Keys and values are written raw with a comma separator and newline record terminator, with no escaping, quoting, or validation on either. Any key containing a comma, or any value containing a newline, produces a file that parses back into different data than was written. Nothing rejects such input at write time, so corruption is introduced silently and only surfaces on a later read.

payload_or_id.name: Store file grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows. Since every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites the whole file, cost per operation on both paths rises linearly with total keys ever written, and the non-atomic-rewrite risk window widens with it. Nothing measures or reports file size or key count.

payload_or_id.name: Every cache miss reads and scans the entire file
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get calls read_text() on the whole file and iterates lines until it matches, with no index, offset map, or streaming. Reading one key costs the full dataset in I/O and allocation. This is the structural reason the latency chain exists and the reason a cold cache is expensive rather than merely slower.

payload_or_id.name: Metrics never reach a scrape endpoint, silently disabling all alerting
payload_or_id.description: The Counter is registered in api.py, but nothing in this repo starts an HTTP exposition server, calls start_http_server, or pushes to a gateway. If the surrounding deployment does not wire one up, the counter increments into a registry nobody reads. This is the failure mode that disables every other detection in this analysis: alert rules on absent series do not fire, so the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. Rated critical because its consequence is the silent loss of the entire alerting capability, and it must be verified rather than assumed before any phase 4 recommendation can be trusted.

payload_or_id.name: Write path emits no signal at all
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value increments no counter, records no latency, and logs nothing on success or failure. Write volume, write errors, and the time since the last successful write are all unobservable, so a write path that has stopped entirely looks exactly like one with nothing to do. Every staleness and data-loss chain in this document originates here and is undetectable at its origin.

payload_or_id.name: StorageError on write is neither caught nor recorded by the service
payload_or_id.description: update_value lets StorageError propagate to its caller with no counter, no log, and no re-raise wrapping. Whether that failure is ever noticed depends entirely on the out-of-repo sync job's own error handling; if it swallows or retries silently, writes can fail indefinitely while the service serves increasingly outdated data and reports every read as a success.

payload_or_id.name: Cache emits no hit, miss, size, or eviction signal
payload_or_id.description: Cache exposes no metrics of any kind. Entry count, hit/miss ratio, and read-through rate are all invisible, which is what makes the unbounded-growth chain undetectable before the OOM kill and makes it impossible to tell whether a stable error rate reflects a healthy backend or merely a cache warm enough that reads never reach it.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass discards the one number it computes
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass returns the count of evicted keys with a docstring stating the purpose is so a caller can observe progress, but nothing records it -- no counter, no log, no last-run timestamp. The result is that both evictor failure modes are silent: a broken pass returning 0 forever and a pass that stopped being scheduled produce byte-identical evidence, namely none.

payload_or_id.name: Upstream data-sync job stops writing
payload_or_id.description: The periodic job that drives update_value is the only writer. If it stops, crashes, or is descheduled, storage quietly freezes at its last state and the whole system serves indefinitely old data while every component reports healthy. The job is out of repo, so the only place its liveness could be inferred from inside the service is a write-side signal, which does not exist -- see fm-write-path-uninstrumented.

result.message: failure-modes.yaml: failure mode 'fm-stale-read-served''s 'coverage_status' must be one of ['alertable', 'metric-gap', 'excluded'], got None

event.text: `coverage_status` is required. Adding it, with the exclusion reasoning stated in-line for the three I'm marking `excluded`.

payload_or_id.name: Client reads a permanently stale value after a write
payload_or_id.description: get_value returns a value that was correct before the last write and is now wrong, and keeps returning it for the life of the process. Cache.get short-circuits on any resident key and never re-consults storage, so once a key is cached the only ways it can ever change are eviction or a restart. Neither happens: the write path does not invalidate, and the evictor's TTL check can never fire. The service reports outcome="success" for every one of these reads.

payload_or_id.name: Client reads None forever for a key that does exist in storage
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get caches the result of a miss, storing Entry(value=None) for keys absent from storage. If a key is read before the data-sync job writes it, the None is cached and served indefinitely afterwards -- the later write to storage cannot dislodge it. This is a distinct outcome from stale-value staleness because the key never had a correct cached value to go stale: a single premature read permanently hides a key from every client. Indistinguishable at the entrypoint from a legitimately absent key, since both return None with outcome="success".

payload_or_id.name: Process is OOM-killed, taking the service down
payload_or_id.description: The cache holds every key ever requested, so under sustained unique-key traffic resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed by the OOM killer or the container's memory limit. Every in-flight request fails and the service is unavailable until it restarts -- at which point the cache is empty and the climb begins again, giving a sawtooth of periodic outages whose interval depends only on traffic mix. Nothing in the process observes its own memory or entry count, so the first signal is the kill itself.

payload_or_id.name: get_value raises StorageError to the client
payload_or_id.description: A read that misses the cache reaches Storage.get, which converts any OSError into StorageError; api.py increments outcome="error" and re-raises to the caller. This is the one failure mode the service instruments today and the only one alertable without new instrumentation. Note the coupling to cache state: with a warm cache only miss traffic is affected, so a completely unreadable backing file can present as a partial rather than total failure, and its blast radius grows immediately after any restart.

payload_or_id.name: Client reads a corrupted or foreign value from delimiter collision
payload_or_id.description: The store's line format is unescaped "key,value" split on the first comma. A value containing a comma round-trips intact, but a key containing a comma is silently re-partitioned on read: writing key "a,b" with value "x" produces the line "a,b,x", which reads back as key "a" with value "b,x". A value containing a newline is worse -- it writes a spurious extra line that becomes a phantom key/value pair, and can shadow or overwrite a real key on the next put(). The result is a client receiving a well-formed value that belongs to a different key, reported as outcome="success". Silent data corruption with no signal at any layer.

payload_or_id.name: Previously written keys disappear from the store
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put rewrites the entire file from an in-memory dict via a single write_text, with no temp-file-and-rename and no lock. A crash, kill, or ENOSPC partway through leaves the file truncated or partially written, destroying keys that were never touched by the write that failed -- the blast radius of one bad write is the whole dataset. Clients see previously-good keys start returning None, or an unparseable tail. Recovery requires a restore; the service itself neither detects nor reports the loss.

payload_or_id.name: Read latency degrades as the store file grows
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads the entire file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size) and the whole file is allocated per miss. This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after a restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been. There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so this manifests to clients as slow reads with no corresponding signal.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass evicts nothing due to a seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in epoch seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, which cache.py sets to `time.time() * 1000`. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS, so expired_keys is always empty and the pass always returns 0. The single mechanism that bounds cache memory and the single mechanism that eventually corrects a stale entry are the same mechanism, and it is dead. Rated critical despite not being user-visible because it is the shared root of both the OOM chain and the staleness chain, and it is the earliest point at which either can be detected.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass is a plain function; the scheduler loop that should call it periodically lives outside this repo. If that loop is missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged, eviction simply never runs. This is a separate failure from the unit mismatch and produces identical downstream effects, which matters for detection: a pass that returns 0 and a pass that never ran are indistinguishable unless the pass itself emits a signal on every execution. Fixing the unit bug alone leaves this failure entirely undetectable.

payload_or_id.name: Write path does not invalidate the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value takes a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put, never cache.evict(key). The seam needed to fix it already exists and is documented in cache.py as intended for exactly this caller. On its own this would bound staleness to one TTL period; combined with the dead evictor it makes staleness permanent. The unused parameter is the tell -- the invalidation was designed and then not wired.

payload_or_id.name: Cache entry count and footprint grow without bound
payload_or_id.description: Entries are only ever added, never removed, so the dict grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys ever requested. Growth rate is set by the unique-key rate rather than the request rate, which means a scan, a crawler, or a key namespace with high cardinality drives it far faster than normal traffic would suggest. This is the observable precursor to the OOM kill and the point at which the chain can be caught with hours or days of warning instead of none.

payload_or_id.name: Cache has no maximum size or replacement policy
payload_or_id.description: Cache is a bare dict with no capacity limit and no LRU/LFU replacement, so there is no backstop if the evictor is broken or stalled: the memory bound rests entirely on an external background job. EXCLUDED FROM ALERTING: this is a static design property, true at every instant from process start, not a condition a system can transition into -- an alert on it would fire constantly or never, and neither carries information. It is a code-fix item (bound the cache so eviction becomes an optimisation rather than a safety mechanism), and its runtime consequence is detected by the entry-count signal on fm-cache-unbounded-growth.

payload_or_id.name: Cache stores negative results indefinitely
payload_or_id.description: On a storage miss, Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) rather than declining to cache. Two consequences: an attacker or a buggy client requesting random non-existent keys inflates the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain; and a key read before it is first written is permanently pinned to None. Negative caching is a legitimate design choice, but only with a TTL, and this cache has no working expiry. Kept as a metric gap rather than excluded because the share of cached entries holding None is a real, varying runtime quantity that distinguishes ordinary growth from miss-driven inflation.

payload_or_id.name: Full cache loss on restart causes a read-through stampede
payload_or_id.description: The cache is process-local with no warming or persistence, so every restart -- including the OOM-kill restarts this design produces -- empties it, and every subsequent request is a miss that scans the whole store file. Storage load and latency therefore spike hardest exactly when the service is recovering. EXCLUDED FROM ALERTING: a restart is an expected, routine event, and paging on one would be noise; the condition that actually needs attention is the latency spike that follows, which is alerted via fm-read-latency-degradation, and the abnormal restarts themselves are alerted via fm-process-oom-crash. Documented because it explains why the latency and OOM chains reinforce each other.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file unreadable (permissions, I/O error, unmounted volume)
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get raises OSError -- and hence StorageError -- if the file exists but cannot be read: permission change, hardware or network-volume I/O error, unmounted path, or exhausted file descriptors. Note the asymmetry deliberately built into get(): a file that does not exist at all returns None rather than raising, so a lost or wrong path presents as every key having silently vanished rather than as an error. That variant is the more dangerous one, because it produces outcome="success" for every read and is covered instead by fm-storage-data-loss.

payload_or_id.name: Filesystem full or out of inodes on write
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put must materialise the entire dataset as a single string and write it in one call, so it needs free space of the order of the whole file on every single write, and briefly holds the dataset twice in memory. On ENOSPC the write_text fails partway, leaving the file truncated -- the non-atomic rewrite converts a full disk directly into dataset-wide data loss rather than into a rejected write.

payload_or_id.name: put() rewrites the whole file in place without atomic replace
payload_or_id.description: write_text truncates the target and writes in place, with no write-to-temp-and-rename and no fsync, so any interruption between truncation and completion leaves a partial file, and the vulnerable window grows with the dataset. EXCLUDED FROM ALERTING: like the missing cache bound, this is a static property of the code rather than a runtime state, so there is no series that could distinguish 'has this defect' from 'does not' -- it emits no signal until it actually tears, at which point fm-storage-data-loss and fm-storage-torn-read carry the detection. It is a code-fix item (write to a temp file and os.replace), and it is the reason those two downstream alerts are needed at all.

payload_or_id.name: Reader observes the file mid-rewrite
payload_or_id.description: With no locking between get() and put(), a read overlapping a rewrite can see a truncated or partially written file. The read then returns None for keys that exist (they were in the not-yet-written tail) or raises StorageError on an I/O failure. Because misses are cached, a None read during this window is captured into the cache and outlives the rewrite that caused it -- a transient storage race is promoted into permanent wrong state.

payload_or_id.name: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: put() is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file. Two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish discards every key the first added. There is no lock, no compare-and-swap, and no version check, and both writers report success. Whether this can fire depends on the deployment -- a single-threaded sync job makes it unreachable -- so it warrants confirming the concurrency model rather than assuming either way.

payload_or_id.name: Unescaped delimiter format does not round-trip keys or values
payload_or_id.description: Keys and values are written raw with a comma separator and newline record terminator, with no escaping, quoting, or validation on either. Any key containing a comma, or any value containing a newline, produces a file that parses back into different data than was written. Nothing rejects such input at write time, so corruption is introduced silently and only surfaces on a later read.

payload_or_id.name: Store file grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows. Since every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites the whole file, cost per operation on both paths rises linearly with total keys ever written, and the non-atomic-rewrite risk window widens with it. Nothing measures or reports file size or key count.

payload_or_id.name: Every cache miss reads and scans the entire file
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get calls read_text() on the whole file and iterates lines until it matches, with no index, offset map, or streaming, so reading one key costs the full dataset in I/O and allocation. EXCLUDED FROM ALERTING: this is the intended (if poor) algorithm rather than a fault -- it is unconditionally true, so no alert can distinguish healthy from unhealthy on it. What varies, and therefore what is alerted, is the resulting miss latency (fm-read-latency-degradation) and the file size driving it (fm-storage-file-unbounded-growth). Documented because it is the structural reason those two matter.

payload_or_id.name: Metrics never reach a scrape endpoint, silently disabling all alerting
payload_or_id.description: The Counter is registered in api.py, but nothing in this repo starts an HTTP exposition server, calls start_http_server, or pushes to a gateway. If the surrounding deployment does not wire one up, the counter increments into a registry nobody reads. This is the failure mode that disables every other detection in this analysis: alert rules on absent series do not fire, so the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. Rated critical because its consequence is the silent loss of the entire alerting capability, and it must be verified rather than assumed before any phase 4 recommendation can be trusted.

Write volume, write errors, and the time since the last successful write are all unobservable, so a write path that has stopped entirely looks exactly like one with nothing to do. Every staleness and data-loss chain in this document originates here and is undetectable at its origin.

payload_or_id.title: StorageError on write is neither caught nor recorded by the service
payload_or_id.description: update_value lets StorageError propagate to its caller with no counter, no log, and no re-raise wrapping. Whether that failure is ever noticed depends entirely on the out-of-repo sync job's own error handling; if it swallows or retries silently, writes can fail indefinitely while the service serves increasingly outdated data and reports every read as a success.

payload_or_id.title: Cache emits no hit, miss, size, or eviction signal
payload_or_id.description: Cache exposes no metrics of any kind. Entry count, hit/miss ratio, and read-through rate are all invisible, which is what makes the unbounded-growth chain undetectable before the OOM kill and makes it impossible to tell whether a stable error rate reflects a healthy backend or merely a cache warm enough that reads never reach it.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass discards the one number it computes
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass returns the count of evicted keys with a docstring stating the purpose is so a caller can observe progress, but nothing records it -- no counter, no log, no last-run timestamp. The result is that both evictor failure modes are silent: a broken pass returning 0 forever and a pass that stopped being scheduled produce byte-identical evidence, namely none.

payload_or_id.title: Upstream data-sync job stops writing
payload_or_id.description: The periodic job that drives update_value is the only writer. If it stops, crashes, or is descheduled, storage quietly freezes at its last state and the whole system serves indefinitely old data while every component reports healthy. The job is out of repo, so the only place its liveness could be inferred from inside the service is a write-side signal, which does not exist -- see fm-write-path-uninstrumented.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads a permanently stale value after a write
payload_or_id.description: get_value returns a value that was correct before the last write and is now wrong, and keeps returning it for the life of the process. Cache.get short-circuits on any resident key and never re-consults storage, so once a key is cached the only ways it can ever change are eviction or a restart. Neither happens: the write path does not invalidate, and the evictor's TTL check can never fire. The service reports outcome="success" for every one of these reads.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads None forever for a key that does exist in storage
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get caches the result of a miss, storing Entry(value=None) for keys absent from storage. If a key is read before the data-sync job writes it, the None is cached and served indefinitely afterwards -- the later write to storage cannot dislodge it. This is a distinct outcome from stale-value staleness because the key never had a correct cached value to go stale: a single premature read permanently hides a key from every client. Indistinguishable at the entrypoint from a legitimately absent key, since both return None with outcome="success".

payload_or_id.title: Process is OOM-killed, taking the service down
payload_or_id.description: The cache holds every key ever requested, so under sustained unique-key traffic resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed by the OOM killer or the container's memory limit. Every in-flight request fails and the service is unavailable until it restarts -- at which point the cache is empty and the climb begins again, giving a sawtooth of periodic outages whose interval depends only on traffic mix. Nothing in the process observes its own memory or entry count, so the first signal is the kill itself.

payload_or_id.title: get_value raises StorageError to the client
payload_or_id.description: A read that misses the cache reaches Storage.get, which converts any OSError into StorageError; api.py increments outcome="error" and re-raises to the caller. This is the one failure mode the service instruments today and the only one alertable without new instrumentation. Note the coupling to cache state: with a warm cache only miss traffic is affected, so a completely unreadable backing file can present as a partial rather than total failure, and its blast radius grows immediately after any restart.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads a corrupted or foreign value from delimiter collision
payload_or_id.description: The store's line format is unescaped "key,value" split on the first comma. A value containing a comma round-trips intact, but a key containing a comma is silently re-partitioned on read: writing key "a,b" with value "x" produces the line "a,b,x", which reads back as key "a" with value "b,x". A value containing a newline is worse -- it writes a spurious extra line that becomes a phantom key/value pair, and can shadow or overwrite a real key on the next put(). The result is a client receiving a well-formed value that belongs to a different key, reported as outcome="success". Silent data corruption with no signal at any layer.

payload_or_id.title: Previously written keys disappear from the store
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put rewrites the entire file from an in-memory dict via a single write_text, with no temp-file-and-rename and no lock. A crash, kill, or ENOSPC partway through leaves the file truncated or partially written, destroying keys that were never touched by the write that failed -- the blast radius of one bad write is the whole dataset. Clients see previously-good keys start returning None, or an unparseable tail. Recovery requires a restore; the service itself neither detects nor reports the loss. A lost or misconfigured file path presents identically, since Storage.get returns None rather than raising when the file is absent.

payload_or_id.title: Read latency degrades as the store file grows
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads the entire file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size) and the whole file is allocated per miss. This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after a restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been. There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so this manifests to clients as slow reads with no corresponding signal.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass evicts nothing due to a seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in epoch seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, which cache.py sets to `time.time() * 1000`. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS, so expired_keys is always empty and the pass always returns 0. The single mechanism that bounds cache memory and the single mechanism that eventually corrects a stale entry are the same mechanism, and it is dead. Rated critical despite not being user-visible because it is the shared root of both the OOM chain and the staleness chain, and it is the earliest point at which either can be detected.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass is a plain function; the scheduler loop that should call it periodically lives outside this repo. If that loop is missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged, eviction simply never runs. This is a separate failure from the unit mismatch and produces identical downstream effects, which matters for detection: a pass that returns 0 and a pass that never ran are indistinguishable unless the pass itself emits a signal on every execution. Fixing the unit bug alone leaves this failure entirely undetectable.

payload_or_id.title: Write path does not invalidate the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value takes a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put, never cache.evict(key). The seam needed to fix it already exists and is documented in cache.py as intended for exactly this caller. On its own this would bound staleness to one TTL period; combined with the dead evictor it makes staleness permanent. The unused parameter is the tell -- the invalidation was designed and then not wired.

payload_or_id.title: Cache entry count and footprint grow without bound
payload_or_id.description: Entries are only ever added, never removed, so the dict grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys ever requested. Growth rate is set by the unique-key rate rather than the request rate, which means a scan, a crawler, or a key namespace with high cardinality drives it far faster than normal traffic would suggest. This is the observable precursor to the OOM kill and the point at which the chain can be caught with hours or days of warning instead of none.

payload_or_id.title: Cache has no maximum size or replacement policy
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Static design property, not a runtime state: it is true at every instant from process start, so an alert on it would fire constantly or never and neither carries information. This is a code-fix item (bound the cache so eviction is an optimisation rather than a safety mechanism), and its runtime consequence is already detected by the entry-count signal on fm-cache-unbounded-growth.
payload_or_id.description: Cache is a bare dict with no capacity limit and no LRU/LFU replacement, so there is no backstop if the evictor is broken or stalled: the memory bound rests entirely on an external background job that this analysis has already found to be non-functional.

payload_or_id.title: Cache stores negative results indefinitely
payload_or_id.description: On a storage miss, Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) rather than declining to cache. Two consequences: an attacker or a buggy client requesting random non-existent keys inflates the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain; and a key read before it is first written is permanently pinned to None. Negative caching is a legitimate design choice, but only with a TTL, and this cache has no working expiry. Kept as a metric gap rather than excluded because the share of cached entries holding None is a real, varying runtime quantity that distinguishes ordinary growth from miss-driven inflation.

payload_or_id.title: Full cache loss on restart causes a read-through stampede
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: A restart is an expected, routine event, so alerting on cache loss itself would page on normal operation. The two conditions that actually warrant attention are both alerted elsewhere: the post-restart latency spike via fm-read-latency-degradation, and abnormal restarts via fm-process-oom-crash. Documented rather than dropped because it explains why the latency and OOM chains reinforce each other -- each memory-exhaustion crash is followed by the worst-case latency window.
payload_or_id.description: The cache is process-local with no warming or persistence, so every restart empties it and every subsequent request is a miss that scans the whole store file. Storage load and read latency therefore spike hardest exactly when the service is recovering.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file unreadable (permissions, I/O error, unmounted volume)
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get raises OSError -- and hence StorageError -- if the file exists but cannot be read: permission change, hardware or network-volume I/O error, unmounted path, or exhausted file descriptors. Note the asymmetry deliberately built into get(): a file that does not exist at all returns None rather than raising, so a lost or wrong path presents as every key having silently vanished rather than as an error. That variant is the more dangerous one, because it produces outcome="success" for every read and is covered instead by fm-storage-data-loss.

payload_or_id.title: Filesystem full or out of inodes on write
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put must materialise the entire dataset as a single string and write it in one call, so it needs free space of the order of the whole file on every single write, and briefly holds the dataset twice in memory. On ENOSPC the write_text fails partway, leaving the file truncated -- the non-atomic rewrite converts a full disk directly into dataset-wide data loss rather than into a rejected write.

payload_or_id.title: put() rewrites the whole file in place without atomic replace
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Static property of the code rather than a runtime state, so no series could distinguish 'has this defect' from 'does not' -- it emits no signal at all until it actually tears, at which point fm-storage-data-loss and fm-storage-torn-read carry the detection. It is a code-fix item (write to a temp file and os.replace, then fsync), and it is precisely the reason those two downstream alerts are needed.
payload_or_id.description: write_text truncates the target and writes in place, with no write-to-temp-and-rename and no fsync, so any interruption between truncation and completion -- crash, OOM kill, deploy, ENOSPC -- leaves a partial file. The vulnerable window is proportional to dataset size, so the risk grows as the store grows, and it also lets a concurrent reader observe the file mid-rewrite.

payload_or_id.title: Reader observes the file mid-rewrite
payload_or_id.description: With no locking between get() and put(), a read overlapping a rewrite can see a truncated or partially written file. The read then returns None for keys that exist (they were in the not-yet-written tail) or raises StorageError on an I/O failure. Because misses are cached, a None read during this window is captured into the cache and outlives the rewrite that caused it -- a transient storage race is promoted into permanent wrong state.

payload_or_id.title: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: put() is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file. Two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish discards every key the first added. There is no lock, no compare-and-swap, and no version check, and both writers report success. Whether this can fire depends on the deployment -- a single-threaded sync job makes it unreachable -- so it warrants confirming the concurrency model rather than assuming either way.

payload_or_id.title: Unescaped delimiter format does not round-trip keys or values
payload_or_id.description: Keys and values are written raw with a comma separator and newline record terminator, with no escaping, quoting, or validation on either. Any key containing a comma, or any value containing a newline, produces a file that parses back into different data than was written. Nothing rejects such input at write time, so corruption is introduced silently and only surfaces on a later read.

payload_or_id.title: Store file grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows. Since every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites the whole file, cost per operation on both paths rises linearly with total keys ever written, and the non-atomic-rewrite risk window widens with it. Nothing measures or reports file size or key count.

payload_or_id.title: Every cache miss reads and scans the entire file
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: This is the intended (if poor) algorithm rather than a fault, and is unconditionally true, so no alert could distinguish healthy from unhealthy on it. What varies -- and is therefore alerted -- is the resulting miss latency (fm-read-latency-degradation) and the file size driving it (fm-storage-file-unbounded-growth). Documented because it is the structural reason those two matter and the reason a cold cache is expensive rather than merely slower.
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get calls read_text() on the whole file and iterates lines until it matches, with no index, offset map, or streaming. Reading one key costs the full dataset in I/O and allocation.

payload_or_id.title: Metrics never reach a scrape endpoint, silently disabling all alerting
payload_or_id.description: The Counter is registered in api.py, but nothing in this repo starts an HTTP exposition server, calls start_http_server, or pushes to a gateway. If the surrounding deployment does not wire one up, the counter increments into a registry nobody reads. This is the failure mode that disables every other detection in this analysis: alert rules on absent series do not fire, so the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. Rated critical because its consequence is the silent loss of the entire alerting capability, and it must be verified rather than assumed before any phase 4 recommendation can be trusted.

event.text:
Phase 2 accepted. 28 failure modes across 6 chains.

**7 user-visible ends, and what feeds them**

| User-visible failure | Sev | Upstream causes |
|---|---|---|
| Permanently stale value after write | crit | no-invalidation + evictor-never-evicts + evictor-not-scheduled |
| `None` forever for a key that exists | crit | caches-misses + no-invalidation + evictor-never-evicts |
| OOM kill (outage) | crit | cache-unbounded-growth |
| `StorageError` to client | crit | filesystem-read-failure + torn-read |
| Corrupted/foreign value returned | crit | delimiter-collision |
| Keys disappear from the store | crit | nonatomic-rewrite + ENOSPC + lost-update |
| Read latency degradation | warn | linear-scan + file-growth + cache-cleared-on-restart |

**Coverage status: 1 of 28 is alertable today.** `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"}` covers the storage-error chain. 23 are metric gaps; 4 are reasoned exclusions.

**The two things worth your attention before phase 3:**

**The evictor bug is load-bearing twice over.** `fm-evictor-never-evicts` is the sole root of both the memory chain and the staleness chain — the same broken TTL comparison is the only bound on cache size *and* the only mechanism that would ever correct a stale entry. That is why I rated it `critical` despite it not being user-visible: it is the earliest single point where two separate critical outages become detectable.

**Three chains produce `outcome="success"` on every affected read.** Staleness, negative-cache poisoning, and delimiter corruption all return a well-formed value through the existing counter. The one metric this service has cannot be made to detect any of them by any alert rule — this is a genuine instrumentation gap, not a threshold-tuning problem.

**Exclusions (4), all for the same structural reason:** `fm-cache-no-size-bound`, `fm-storage-nonatomic-rewrite`, `fm-storage-linear-scan`, and `fm-cache-cleared-on-restart`. The first three are static properties of the code — unconditionally true from process start, so no series can distinguish healthy from unhealthy and any alert fires constantly or never. They are code-fix items whose runtime consequences are alerted downstream. The fourth is excluded because restarts are routine; the latency spike and the abnormal-restart cause are each alerted separately.

**One item I could not resolve from the code:** `fm-concurrent-write-lost-update` depends on whether the out-of-repo sync job is single-threaded. If it is, the mode is unreachable and should become an exclusion in phase 3; if not, it is a live data-loss path. Worth confirming rather than my assuming either way.

Ready for phase 3.

Phase 3 -- metric coverage: inventory the metrics this codebase actually implements as
Metric entries (tied to where each is emitted in the code), then set every failure
mode's coverage status: `alertable` (implemented metrics suffice; only an alert rule is
missing), `metric-gap` (implemented metrics cannot detect it adequately; propose the
metric change needed), or `excluded` (record the reason). Every metric recommendation
must name the failure mode(s) it serves and state whether it is a new metric or a
change to an existing one. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 3.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Inventory instrumentation already implemented in this codebase using any of:

- Python: the `prometheus_client` library (Counter, Gauge, Histogram, Summary
  definitions and their `.labels(...)` call sites).
- Go: `prometheus/client_golang` (`prometheus.NewCounter`/`NewGauge`/`NewHistogram`
  and their registration with a `prometheus.Registry`).
- Node.js: `prom-client` (`new Counter(...)`, `new Gauge(...)`, `new Histogram(...)`).
- Java/JVM: Micrometer's Prometheus registry (`PrometheusMeterRegistry`, meters
  registered against it).
- Any direct `/metrics` HTTP exposition endpoint, whichever library serves it.

A metric definition site is where a metric's name, type, and labels are declared —
not every place it is incremented or observed.
Confirming the instrumentation inventory is complete before proposing.
Confirmed: exactly one metric definition site in the entire repo, and no exposition endpoint of any kind.

payload_or_id.name: Expose the Prometheus registry over HTTP
payload_or_id.title: Wire a /metrics exposition endpoint and verify it is scraped

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_entries
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of current cache entry count
payload_or_id.description: Number of entries currently resident in Cache._entries.
payload_or_id.details: Set the gauge to len(self._entries) after each insertion in Cache.get and each removal in Cache.evict, or register it as a callback gauge so the value is computed at scrape time (cheaper and impossible to drift from reality). payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_negative_entries
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of cached entries holding a None value
payload_or_id.description: Count of resident entries whose value is None -- i.e. cached misses.
payload_or_id.details: Maintain alongside mr-cache-entries, or expose as a callback gauge counting entries with value is None. payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_lookups_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of cache lookups labeled hit or miss
payload_or_id.description: Counts every Cache.get call, labeled result=hit|miss.
payload_or_id.details: Increment result="hit" on the early-return branch at cache.py:33 and result="miss" on the read-through branch at cache.py:34-36. The miss rate is the load actually reaching storage, which is what drives the linear-scan cost, and a step change in miss rate is the signature of a post-restart stampede. payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_oldest_entry_age_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of the age of the oldest resident cache entry
payload_or_id.description: Age in seconds of the oldest entry currently in the cache.
payload_or_id.details: Expose as a callback gauge computing now - min(inserted_at) over resident entries, taking care to divide by 1000 since inserted_at_ms is in milliseconds -- the same unit trap that produced fm-evictor-never-evicts. payload_or_id.rationale: This is the most direct possible statement of the invariant the evictor exists to maintain. Unlike eviction counts, it cannot be satisfied by a pass that runs busily and removes the wrong things, and it stays meaningful after the unit bug is fixed.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_eviction_last_success_timestamp_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Counter of eviction passes plus last-completion timestamp gauge
payload_or_id.description: A kvstore_eviction_passes_total counter incremented on every completed pass, and a kvstore_eviction_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge set to the wall-clock time each pass completes.
payload_or_id.details: Instrument at the end of run_eviction_pass. The timestamp gauge is what makes 'the scheduler stopped calling this' detectable: a stalled pass leaves the gauge frozen while every other series in the system continues to look healthy. Note that the counter alone is insufficient -- alerting on rate(passes_total) == 0 fails to fire when the series stops being reported entirely, whereas time() - the timestamp gauge keeps rising and crosses any threshold.
payload_or_id.rationale: Phase 2 established that a pass returning 0 and a pass that never ran produce identical evidence today. This separates them, which matters because they need different fixes: one is a code bug, the other a deployment fault.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_evicted_keys_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of keys removed by eviction
payload_or_id.description: Total keys evicted, incremented by the return value of run_eviction_pass.
payload_or_id.details: The function already computes exactly this number and its docstring states the purpose is so a caller can observe progress -- nothing records it. Increment by len(expired_keys) before returning. Pair with mr-eviction-pass-liveness: passes running while this counter stays flat is the precise signature of the seconds/milliseconds unit bug, and is what distinguishes it from the scheduler having stopped.
payload_or_id.rationale: Zero-cost to add since the value is already computed, and it is the one signal that would have made the existing unit-mismatch bug visible the day it shipped.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_invalidations_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of cache invalidations labeled by source
payload_or_id.description: Counts Cache.evict calls, labeled source=writer|evictor.
payload_or_id.details: Increment in Cache.evict with a source label supplied by the caller. Writes proceeding while source="writer" invalidations stay at zero is a direct, machine-checkable statement of fm-write-path-no-invalidation -- it detects the missing wiring itself rather than waiting for a user to observe stale data. This depends on mr-storage-operations-total to supply the write count for comparison.
payload_or_id.rationale: Catches the defect at the earliest link in the staleness chain. It also guards the fix: if someone later refactors update_value and drops the invalidation again, the ratio breaks immediately.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_operations_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of storage operations labeled by operation and outcome
payload_or_id.description: Counts every Storage.get and Storage.put, labeled operation=get|put and outcome=success|error.
payload_or_id.details: Instrument inside Storage.get and Storage.put, incrementing outcome="error" in the except OSError branches before raising StorageError. This is the single recommendation that lights up the entire write path, which today emits nothing at all: write volume, write failures, and by absence the liveness of the out-of-repo sync job all become visible. It also separates read-side from write-side storage failure, which the existing api.py counter conflates by only ever seeing the read side.
payload_or_id.rationale: The write path is the origin of every staleness and data-loss chain in this analysis and is currently 100% unobservable. Placing the counter in Storage rather than in admin.py means it cannot be bypassed by a future second writer.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_operation_duration_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Histogram of storage operation latency
payload_or_id.description: Latency distribution of Storage.get and Storage.put, labeled by operation.
payload_or_id.details: Wrap both method bodies with a Histogram timer. Since get() cost is O(file size) and put() reads and rewrites the whole file, this is the metric that turns the structural linear-scan cost into an observable trend and lets a threshold be set on user-facing miss latency rather than on the file size that proxies it. Use buckets that span the expected range from a small file to a degraded one; the defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate.
payload_or_id.rationale: There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service today, so read slowness has no signal at all. Measuring at the storage boundary attributes it to the right layer rather than leaving it as unexplained end-to-end slowness.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_last_successful_write_timestamp_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of the time of the last successful write
payload_or_id.description: Wall-clock timestamp of the most recent successful Storage.put.
payload_or_id.details: Set at the end of the successful path in Storage.put. Alerting on time() minus this gauge is the only way to detect that the out-of-repo sync job has stopped: with no write-side signal the service serves indefinitely frozen data while every component reports healthy. A timestamp gauge is used rather than rate() on a counter because it keeps producing a rising, alertable value even when writes cease entirely.
payload_or_id.rationale: Detects an upstream dependency failure from inside the service, without requiring access to the sync job's own instrumentation, which is out of this repo's control.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_keys
payload_or_id.title: Gauges of stored key count and backing file size
payload_or_id.description: kvstore_storage_keys (number of records in the store) and kvstore_storage_file_bytes (size of the backing file).
payload_or_id.details: Set both at the end of Storage.put, where the full record dict and the serialized payload are already in hand, so neither costs an extra file read. The key count is the only mechanism in this entire analysis capable of detecting fm-storage-data-loss: a truncating write, a torn rewrite, or a lost-update collision all manifest as the count dropping, and since the store has no delete operation, any decrease at all is by definition data loss. The byte gauge drives the growth and latency chains.
payload_or_id.rationale: Data loss is otherwise completely silent -- vanished keys return None with outcome="success", indistinguishable from keys that never existed. A monotonicity invariant on key count is the cheapest way to make it observable.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_invalid_records_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of records rejected or detected as unparseable
payload_or_id.description: Counts keys or values that violate the storage format, labeled reason=key_contains_delimiter|value_contains_newline|unparseable_line.
payload_or_id.details: This recommendation requires a small code change to be meaningful: Storage.put currently accepts any key or value without validation, so there is nothing to count. Add a guard rejecting keys containing a comma and values containing a newline, increment this counter with the reason, and raise rather than silently corrupting the file. Also increment reason="unparseable_line" in get() for any line that fails to partition cleanly, which catches pre-existing corruption on read.
payload_or_id.rationale: Silent corruption is the worst class of failure here because the client receives a well-formed value belonging to a different key and every layer reports success. Converting it into a loud rejection at write time is preferable to detecting it after the fact; the counter exists to prove the guard is holding and to size any pre-existing damage.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_filesystem_free_bytes
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of free space on the volume holding the store
payload_or_id.description: Free bytes on the filesystem containing the storage path.
payload_or_id.details: Expose as a callback gauge using shutil.disk_usage(self._path.parent).free. Check first whether node_exporter or an equivalent already covers this volume -- if it does, prefer that series and skip this recommendation rather than duplicating it, since the node-level metric is better maintained and covers volumes this process never touches. Add it in-process only if the store lives somewhere the node exporter does not observe, or if the deployment has no node-level monitoring.
payload_or_id.rationale: ENOSPC is unusually dangerous here because put() rewrites the whole file: a full disk does not merely reject the write, it truncates the dataset. Free space needs headroom of roughly one full file size, which is a stricter condition than a generic disk alert would use.

payload_or_id.name: process_resident_memory_bytes
payload_or_id.title: Enable default process collectors for memory and restart detection
payload_or_id.description: process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds, supplied automatically by prometheus_client's default collectors.
payload_or_id.details: These require no instrumentation code -- prometheus_client registers them with the default registry automatically, so they arrive as soon as mr-expose-metrics-endpoint is done. Resident memory approaching the container limit is the last-line signal for the OOM chain, and a change in process_start_time_seconds detects the restart after a kill has already happened. Treat both as backstops behind mr-cache-entries, which fires far earlier.
payload_or_id.rationale: Listed explicitly despite being free because it would otherwise be assumed present. Memory alone is a poor primary signal here: it fires late and does not attribute the growth to the cache, but it does catch leaks the cache gauge would miss.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_write_conflicts_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of detected concurrent-write conflicts (conditional)
payload_or_id.description: Counts writes that detected a competing modification of the backing file.
payload_or_id.details: CONDITIONAL -- confirm the deployment's concurrency model before implementing. If the out-of-repo sync job is single-threaded and is the only writer, fm-concurrent-write-lost-update is unreachable and this metric should be dropped rather than built. If concurrent writers are possible, the metric cannot be implemented alone: it requires first adding the conflict detection it counts (an advisory lock via fcntl.flock, or comparing the file's mtime/size between the read and the write inside put()). Increment when a competing modification is observed.
payload_or_id.rationale: Recorded as an open question rather than resolved either way, because the code cannot answer it and guessing wrong is costly in both directions -- building unnecessary locking, or leaving a silent data-loss path unmonitored.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_get_value_requests_total
payload_or_id.title: Add a found label to the existing request counter
payload_or_id.description: Extend the existing kvstore_get_value_requests_total with a second label, found=true|false, distinguishing reads that returned a value from reads that returned None.
payload_or_id.details: Change to the existing metric defined at kvstore/api.py:19-23: add "found" to the label list and set it from whether the returned value is None at the two increment sites. Cardinality cost is one extra dimension of two values, which is negligible. Today a read returning None and a read returning a value are both counted identically as outcome="success", so the service cannot distinguish serving data from serving nothing. A sustained rise in found="false" is the client-side signature of both negative-cache poisoning and mass data loss.
payload_or_id.rationale: The cheapest change in this phase and the only one to an existing metric. It does not by itself prove which of the two causes is responsible -- that needs mr-storage-size-and-keys and mr-cache-negative-entries -- but it is the signal that says something is wrong from the user's point of view, which the current counter cannot express at all.
