payload_or_id.description: Extend the existing kvstore_get_value_requests_total with a second label, found=true|false, distinguishing reads that returned a value from reads that returned None.
payload_or_id.details: Change to the existing metric defined at kvstore/api.py:19-23: add "found" to the label list and set it from whether the returned value is None at the two increment sites. Cardinality cost is one extra dimension of two values, which is negligible. Today a read returning None and a read returning a value are both counted identically as outcome="success", so the service cannot distinguish serving data from serving nothing. A sustained rise in found="false" is the client-side signature of both negative-cache poisoning and mass data loss.
payload_or_id.rationale: The cheapest change in this phase and the only one to an existing metric. It does not by itself prove which of the two causes is responsible -- that needs mr-storage-size-and-keys and mr-cache-negative-entries -- but it is the signal that says something is wrong from the user's point of view, which the current counter cannot express at all.

event.text: Now the coverage decision for each of the 28 failure modes.

payload_or_id.rationale: kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} increments on exactly this failure; only an alert rule is missing. Caveat for phase 4: because cache hits never reach storage, this counter under-reports a storage outage in proportion to cache warmth, so the rule should trigger on error ratio against total requests rather than absolute rate. mr-storage-operations-total would improve attribution but is not required for detection.

Every OSError on read becomes a StorageError and is already counted as outcome="error", so this is detectable today with a rule alone. Note the limit of that coverage: it catches the file being present but unreadable, not the file being absent, because Storage.get returns None rather than raising in that case -- that variant is covered under fm-storage-data-loss. mr-storage-operations-total would separate read-side from write-side filesystem failure, which the entrypoint counter cannot do.

The existing counter reports outcome="success" for every stale read, so no alert rule over current instrumentation can detect this at any threshold. Detection must move upstream: mr-cache-oldest-entry-age proves entries are outliving the TTL, and mr-cache-invalidations-total proves writes are not invalidating. Neither observes staleness directly -- that would require comparing cached against stored values -- but together they detect both mechanisms that produce it.

Today a poisoned None and a legitimately absent key are byte-identical at the only instrumented point: both are outcome="success" with no indication a value was even returned. mr-get-value-found-label makes the user-visible symptom countable, and mr-cache-negative-entries sizes the at-risk population. Full certainty still requires correlating a found=false read against a key present in storage, which no single metric can express; these two make the condition visible enough to investigate.

Nothing observes memory or entry count, so the first evidence today is the kill itself -- and after restart the counter resumes from zero looking healthy. mr-cache-entries gives hours-to-days of lead time on the precursor; mr-process-memory-and-restarts is the late backstop and confirms the kill happened. The precursor is the one worth alerting on.

Corrupted values are well-formed strings returned as outcome="success"; no existing or proposed metric can detect that a returned value belongs to a different key. This is therefore covered by prevention plus a proof-of-guard counter rather than by detection: mr-storage-invalid-records requires adding write-time validation, which converts silent corruption into a loud rejection. Stated plainly because it is the one failure mode here where instrumentation alone is not a sufficient answer.

Vanished keys return None with outcome="success", indistinguishable from keys that never existed, so this is entirely invisible today. mr-storage-size-and-keys is the only proposal capable of detecting it: the store has no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and any drop is by definition data loss. That invariant makes for an unusually precise alert.

There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so slow reads produce no signal at all -- the request counter records that a call happened, never how long it took. mr-storage-operation-duration measures the user-facing symptom directly; the other two explain it (miss volume and file size) and are what make the alert actionable rather than merely true.

The evictor emits nothing, so a pass that removes zero entries forever is completely silent. mr-evicted-keys-total costs nothing to add because run_eviction_pass already computes the number and discards it. mr-cache-oldest-entry-age is the stronger signal: it asserts the invariant the evictor exists to maintain, so it stays valid after the unit bug is fixed and catches any future regression that leaves eviction running but ineffective.

Not detectable today by any means, and specifically not separable from fm-evictor-never-evicts. mr-eviction-pass-liveness resolves that: the last-completion timestamp gauge keeps producing a rising, alertable value when the pass stops entirely, which a rate() over a counter does not. The two failure modes need different fixes -- a code change versus a deployment fix -- which is why distinguishing them is worth a dedicated metric.

The write path emits nothing, so the missing invalidation is invisible until a user reads stale data. Together these two make the defect itself machine-checkable: writes occurring while source="writer" invalidations remain at zero states the bug directly. This is the earliest detectable link in the staleness chain and also guards against the fix being dropped in a later refactor.

No metric observes cache size. mr-cache-entries covers this directly and is the highest-value single addition in the analysis, since this failure mode is the sole cause of the OOM outage and gives long lead time. mr-cache-negative-entries separates miss-driven inflation from legitimate working-set growth, which matters because the two call for different remedies.

Not observable today. Kept as a gap rather than an exclusion because, unlike the missing size bound, the count of resident None entries is a genuinely varying runtime quantity: it distinguishes an adversarial or buggy key-space probe from ordinary growth, and it sizes the population of keys at risk of permanent None-pinning.

Write-side OSError is entirely uninstrumented today, so a full disk is silent until it has already truncated the dataset. mr-storage-operations-total catches the failed write; mr-filesystem-free-bytes catches it before it happens. Note the headroom needed here is roughly one whole file size, because put() rewrites the entire store -- a generic disk-space alert tuned to a percentage may fire too late.

A torn read surfaces either as a StorageError (already counted at the entrypoint, though not attributed to this cause) or as a silent None that then gets cached and outlives the race. The silent path is the dangerous one and is invisible today. These two narrow the diagnosis by correlating read errors against concurrent write activity; neither detects the silent variant directly, which is a residual gap worth stating rather than papering over.

OPEN QUESTION, carried from phase 2 and still unresolved by the code: whether concurrent writers exist depends on the out-of-repo sync job's threading model. If it is single-threaded and the only writer, this mode is unreachable and should be reclassified as excluded. If not, it is a live silent data-loss path. The recommendation is explicitly conditional, and it also requires adding the conflict detection it counts -- the metric cannot be built on its own.

Nothing validates keys or values on write, so malformed records enter the store silently and only surface as corruption on a later read. mr-storage-invalid-records requires adding that validation first; the counter then proves the guard is holding and sizes any pre-existing damage found while reading.

Neither file size nor key count is measured. mr-storage-size-and-keys covers this at no extra I/O cost, since both values are already in hand at the end of Storage.put. Growth here compounds two other chains -- read latency and the non-atomic-rewrite risk window -- so it is worth a slow-burn warning rather than being left to the latency alert alone.

Self-referential and therefore worth stating carefully: this cannot be detected by any metric this service emits, because its whole content is that emitted metrics do not arrive. Detection must come from the monitoring system's own view -- Prometheus target UP, or an absent() rule over a series known to be always present. mr-expose-metrics-endpoint is a prerequisite for every other item in this phase, and its verification step is manual by necessity.

This failure mode is the absence of instrumentation itself, so it is a gap by definition. Both recommendations sit in Storage rather than in admin.py deliberately: instrumenting the datastore boundary cannot be bypassed by a future second writer, whereas instrumenting the one known caller can.

StorageError from put() propagates into out-of-repo code with no counter, log, or trace inside the service. mr-storage-operations-total with outcome="error" on operation="put" makes write failures visible from inside this service, which matters because whether the sync job reports its own errors is outside this codebase's control and cannot be assumed.

The cache emits nothing at all. Beyond enabling the growth and staleness chains, the hit/miss counter fixes a subtle blind spot in the metric that does exist: a flat error rate cannot currently distinguish a healthy backend from a cache warm enough that storage is never exercised, meaning storage could be entirely broken while the service looks fine.

The pass computes the eviction count expressly so a caller can observe progress, per its own docstring, and then nothing records it. Recording it plus a completion timestamp is the minimum that makes the evictor's two failure modes distinguishable from each other and from healthy operation.

A frozen upstream job is invisible from inside the service today: no write-side signal exists, so 'nothing to write' and 'not running' look identical. mr-last-successful-write-timestamp detects it without needing access to the job's own instrumentation. Threshold must be derived from the job's expected cadence, which is not knowable from this repo -- flagged for phase 4.

payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Static design property rather than a runtime state: true at every instant from process start, so any alert on it fires constantly or never and neither carries information. It is a code-fix item -- bound the cache so eviction becomes an optimisation rather than a load-bearing safety mechanism -- and its runtime consequence is fully covered by mr-cache-entries under fm-cache-unbounded-growth.
payload_or_id.rationale: Excluded from alerting, not from the fix list. The absence of a capacity bound is why a single background-job bug escalates to an outage.

payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Restarts are expected, routine events; alerting on cache loss itself would page on normal operation. Both conditions that actually warrant attention are alerted elsewhere: the post-restart latency spike under fm-read-latency-degradation, and abnormal restarts under fm-process-oom-crash via process_start_time_seconds.
payload_or_id.rationale: Retained in the document because it explains why the OOM and latency chains reinforce each other: every memory-exhaustion crash is followed immediately by the worst-case cold-cache latency window.

payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Static property of the code, not a runtime state -- no series can distinguish 'has this defect' from 'does not', and it emits no signal at all until it actually tears. At that point detection is carried by mr-storage-size-and-keys under fm-storage-data-loss and by mr-storage-operations-total under fm-storage-torn-read. It is a code-fix item: write to a temp file, fsync, then os.replace.
payload_or_id.rationale: Excluded from alerting but arguably the highest-value code fix in the storage layer, since it is the reason a single interrupted write can destroy the entire dataset.

payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: This is the intended algorithm rather than a fault, and is unconditionally true on every read, so no alert could distinguish healthy from unhealthy on it. What varies -- and is alerted -- is the resulting latency (mr-storage-operation-duration) and the file size driving it (mr-storage-size-and-keys).
payload_or_id.rationale: Documented because it is the structural reason the latency chain exists and why a cold cache is expensive rather than merely slower; the alerting is correctly placed on its symptoms.

event.text:
Phase 3 accepted: 1 metric inventoried, 17 recommendations, 28 coverage decisions.

**Implemented instrumentation — the complete inventory**

`kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}`, a Counter defined at `kvstore/api.py:19-23`, incremented at lines 30 and 32. That is the whole of it. I grepped the repo for every library form in scope — `prometheus_client`, and any exposition endpoint — and there is exactly one definition site and **no exposition path at all**: no `start_http_server`, no `make_wsgi_app`, no `generate_latest`, no `/metrics` handler.

That second finding is the one I'd act on first. The counter is registered against the default registry and increments correctly, but nothing in this repo makes it reachable. If the surrounding deployment doesn't wire exposition up, every alert rule written against it evaluates over a series that doesn't exist — and an absent series doesn't fail loudly, it silently never fires. **This needs to be verified by scraping the endpoint by hand, not inferred from code.**

**Coverage: 2 alertable, 22 metric-gap, 4 excluded**

Only the storage-error chain is alertable today (`fm-read-storage-error-to-client`, `fm-filesystem-read-failure`) — one rule, no new instrumentation.

**Where the existing metric is structurally unable to help.** Three chains — staleness, negative-cache poisoning, delimiter corruption — return well-formed values as `outcome="success"`. No threshold on the current counter detects any of them. Detection has to move upstream, which is what most of the recommendations do.

**Highest-leverage additions**, in order:

1. `mr-cache-entries` — turns the OOM outage from undetectable-until-the-kill into a trend with days of lead time.
2. `mr-storage-operations-total` — lights up the entire write path, currently 100% dark. Placed in `Storage`, not `admin.py`, so a future second writer can't bypass it.
3. `mr-storage-size-and-keys` — the store has no delete, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing *by construction*; any drop is by definition data loss. An unusually precise alert.
4. `mr-evicted-keys-total` — free: `run_eviction_pass` already computes the number and throws it away.

**Two places where instrumentation alone is not the answer, stated rather than glossed:**

- `fm-wrong-value-returned` — no metric can detect that a returned value belongs to a different key. Covered by *prevention* (write-time validation) plus a proof-of-guard counter.
- `fm-metrics-not-exposed` — self-referential; cannot be detected by any metric this service emits. Detection must come from Prometheus's own target view.

**Two open items for phase 4:** the concurrency model behind `fm-concurrent-write-lost-update` (unresolved from phase 2 — if the sync job is single-threaded this becomes an exclusion), and the sync job's expected cadence, which sets the threshold for `mr-last-successful-write-timestamp` and isn't knowable from this repo.

Ready for phase 4.

Phase 4 -- alert recommendations: for every non-excluded failure mode, recommend at
least one alert rule detecting it, naming the failure mode(s) it serves; an alert
serving several failure modes carries the highest severity among them. No failure mode
may go silently unmapped. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 4.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields
populated:

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most
  5000 characters. Split an alert that would need more into
  several smaller ones rather than writing one long expression.
- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus
  duration (e.g. `5m`).
- `severity`: `critical` or `warning`, matching the failure mode's severity.
- `annotations`: a dict whose required keys are `summary` (a short one-line
  description) and `description` (the fuller explanation shown on the alert).
All 24 non-excluded failure modes mapped. Proposing 20 alert rules.

annotations.summary: kvstore metrics target is down or has never been scraped
annotations.description: Prometheus cannot scrape kvstore. This alert must exist before any other rule here is trusted: the service defines its Counter but wires no exposition endpoint, so if start_http_server or make_wsgi_app was never called, every other alert in this group evaluates over a non-existent series and silently never fires -- the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. The absent() arm is the load-bearing half: a target that never appeared at all produces no up series to compare against zero. Verify by scraping the endpoint by hand; never infer exposition from the code.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreInstrumentationMissing
payload_or_id.expr:
absent(kvstore_cache_entries)
or absent(kvstore_cache_lookups_total)
or absent(kvstore_evicted_keys_total)
or absent(kvstore_eviction_last_success_timestamp_seconds)
or absent(kvstore_storage_operations_total)
or absent(kvstore_last_successful_write_timestamp_seconds)

annotations.summary: One or more kvstore instrumentation series has stopped being reported
annotations.description: A metric added to close a phase-3 gap is no longer present. This is the dead-man's switch for the instrumentation itself: the cache, evictor, and write path each emitted nothing at all before this work, and a refactor that drops a Gauge or moves a counter out of the code path would silently return them to that state -- with every alert built on them going quiet rather than red. Enable only after the corresponding metrics ship, or it fires immediately. Treat a firing instance as 'the alerts you think you have are gone', not as a metrics-plumbing nuisance.

annotations.summary: Over 1% of get_value calls are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: Clients are receiving errors from the read path. This is the only alert in the group that needs no new instrumentation -- it runs against the counter already defined at kvstore/api.py:19-23. Expressed as a ratio rather than an absolute rate deliberately: cache hits never reach storage, so a completely unreadable backing file presents as a partial failure whose apparent size depends on cache warmth, and an absolute threshold would be calibrated to traffic that may not be reaching storage at all. The trailing rate>0 guard prevents a division-by-zero NaN from suppressing the alert during idle periods. Expect the ratio to jump after any restart, when every read is a miss.

annotations.summary: The storage layer is failing to read the backing file
annotations.description: Storage.get raised OSError -- permission change, I/O error, unmounted volume, exhausted file descriptors -- or read the file while a rewrite was in flight. Fires at the storage boundary rather than at the entrypoint, so it detects the fault even when a warm cache is absorbing most reads and the client-facing error ratio stays below its threshold. Any non-zero count is worth investigating: this path should never fail in normal operation. Note what this does NOT catch: a missing or misconfigured file path, because Storage.get returns None rather than raising when the file is absent -- that variant is covered by KvstoreStoredKeyCountDropped.

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is large and still rising with no sign of eviction
annotations.description: The cache is growing monotonically toward an OOM kill. This is the earliest actionable point in the memory chain and the reason to alert here rather than on memory: it gives hours to days of lead time, and it attributes the growth to the cache rather than to an unspecified leak. The two conditions are both needed -- absolute size alone fires on a legitimately large working set, and positive derivative alone fires on ordinary warm-up. CALIBRATE the 500000 threshold against the container memory limit divided by average entry size before enabling; the value here is a placeholder, not a measurement. Growth is driven by the unique-key rate, not the request rate, so a scan or a crawler moves this far faster than traffic volume suggests.

annotations.summary: kvstore resident memory is within 15% of its limit
annotations.description: The process is approaching an OOM kill, which takes the service down entirely and fails every in-flight request. This is the last-line backstop behind KvstoreCacheEntriesGrowingUnbounded, which fires far earlier -- by the time this one is up there may be minutes rather than hours. Comes free from prometheus_client's default collectors once exposition is wired. If cAdvisor is not present in this deployment, replace the denominator with the literal limit in bytes rather than dropping the alert.

annotations.summary: kvstore has restarted more than three times in six hours
annotations.description: Repeated restarts are the signature of the OOM sawtooth this design produces: the cache fills, the process is killed, it restarts with an empty cache, and the climb begins again on an interval set only by traffic mix. Thresholded at more than three restarts specifically so a routine deploy does not page -- a single restart is expected and is deliberately not alerted on. Each restart also drops the entire cache, so every one of them is followed immediately by the worst-case cold-cache latency window; expect KvstoreReadLatencyHigh to fire alongside this.

annotations.summary: Cached entries are older than twice the configured TTL
annotations.description: An entry older than TTL_SECONDS (300) is by definition one the evictor should have removed, so this asserts the exact invariant the evictor exists to maintain. It is the primary detector for the seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch in evictor.py, and it detects that fault without needing to know whether the pass ran and found nothing or never ran at all. It is also the closest available proxy for stale reads, which are otherwise entirely undetectable -- every stale read is counted as outcome=success, so no rule over the existing counter can find them at any threshold. Because the same broken TTL check is the only bound on cache size AND the only mechanism that corrects a stale entry, this one alert covers the root of two separate critical chains.

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are running but removing no entries while expired ones exist
annotations.description: The precise signature of the unit-mismatch bug: the scheduler is calling run_eviction_pass, the pass completes, and yet nothing is evicted despite entries being past TTL. All three conditions are required -- without the passes term this also fires when the scheduler has stopped (a different fault with a different fix, covered by KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning), and without the age term it fires harmlessly whenever there is genuinely nothing to evict. Diagnostic value beyond detection: this distinguishes 'the code is wrong' from 'the job is not running', which the service today cannot tell apart at all.

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has completed in 15 minutes
annotations.description: The scheduler loop that drives run_eviction_pass lives outside this repo, so it can be missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged with nothing in the service noticing. Written against a last-completion timestamp rather than rate() over a counter for a specific reason: when a job stops entirely its counter stops changing, and a rate-based rule goes quiet rather than firing, whereas time() minus a frozen timestamp keeps rising and crosses any threshold. CALIBRATE the 900s against the scheduler's actual interval (roughly three missed runs is a reasonable starting point); that interval is not knowable from this repo.

annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache invalidation is following them
annotations.description: States the defect in admin.update_value directly: it takes a Cache parameter and never calls cache.evict, so a key already resident keeps serving its pre-write value. Detecting the missing wiring is far better than waiting for a user to notice stale data, which is the only way this surfaces today. This alert will fire immediately on the current code and should stay firing until the invalidation is wired up -- that is the intended behaviour, not a misconfiguration. Once fixed it becomes a regression guard: if a later refactor drops the evict call again, the ratio breaks the same way.

annotations.summary: No successful write to storage in six hours
annotations.description: The periodic data-sync job is the only writer in the system. If it stops, crashes, or is descheduled, storage quietly freezes at its last state and the service serves indefinitely old data while every component reports healthy -- reads keep succeeding, error rates stay flat, and nothing anywhere goes red. This detects an out-of-repo dependency failure from inside the service, without needing access to that job's own instrumentation. CALIBRATE 21600s against the sync job's actual cadence, which is not knowable from this repo -- flagged as an open question in phase 3 and still open.

annotations.summary: Storage writes are failing
annotations.description: Storage.put raised OSError -- most likely a full disk, a permissions change, or an unwritable parent directory. Today this is completely silent inside the service: update_value lets StorageError propagate with no counter and no log, so whether anyone finds out depends entirely on the out-of-repo sync job's error handling, which this codebase does not control. Treat any occurrence as urgent despite the warning severity: because put() rewrites the whole file in place with no atomic replace, a write that fails partway does not merely reject the update, it can truncate the entire dataset.

annotations.summary: The number of keys in the store has decreased -- data has been lost
annotations.description: The store exposes no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and ANY decrease is by definition data loss. That makes this an unusually precise alert: there is no benign explanation to triage past. It is the only mechanism in this entire analysis capable of detecting a truncated or torn rewrite, a lost update from concurrent writers, or a backing file that has been replaced or lost -- all of which are otherwise perfectly silent, because vanished keys return None with outcome=success, indistinguishable from keys that never existed. Investigate immediately and expect to restore from backup; the service will not recover on its own.

annotations.summary: Free disk space is under twice the size of the store file
annotations.description: Thresholded against the store's own size rather than as a percentage of the volume, because that is what the failure actually depends on: Storage.put serialises the entire dataset and writes it in one call, so every single write needs free space of the order of the whole file. A generic 90%-full disk alert can therefore fire far too late on a large store, or far too early on a small one. ENOSPC here is not a rejected write -- the non-atomic rewrite turns a full disk directly into dataset-wide truncation. If node_exporter already covers this volume, prefer its series over adding an in-process gauge.

annotations.summary: A key or value violating the storage format was rejected or found in the store
annotations.description: The store's line format is unescaped key,value split on the first comma, with no validation. A key containing a comma reads back as a different key with a different value, and a value containing a newline writes a phantom record that can shadow a real key. The client then receives a well-formed value belonging to someone else, reported as outcome=success -- silent corruption with no signal at any layer. This is the one failure mode where instrumentation alone is not the answer: the counter only exists once write-time validation is added, and its real job is to prove that guard is holding and to size any corruption already in the file. reason="unparseable_line" indicates pre-existing damage found on read rather than a newly blocked write.

annotations.summary: Over 30% of successful reads are returning no value
annotations.description: The client-side symptom shared by negative-cache poisoning and mass data loss: clients are being told a key does not exist. Requires the found label added to the existing counter -- today a read returning None and a read returning data are counted identically, so the service cannot distinguish serving data from serving nothing. This alert says something is wrong from the user's point of view; it does not identify which cause. Disambiguate with kvstore_cache_negative_entries (poisoning) and kvstore_storage_keys (loss). CALIBRATE 0.3 against the normal miss rate for this key space, which may legitimately be high.

annotations.summary: Most of the cache is cached misses, which never expire
annotations.description: Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) on a miss and the cache has no working expiry, so every cached miss is permanent. Two consequences, both live here: any key read before the sync job first writes it is pinned to None forever and becomes invisible to every client, and an attacker or buggy client probing random keys can inflate the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain. A high and rising negative share is the signature that distinguishes miss-driven inflation from legitimate working-set growth -- which matters because they call for different fixes: rate limiting or refusing to cache negatives, versus a capacity bound.

annotations.summary: p99 storage read latency is above 500ms
annotations.description: Every cache miss reads the entire backing file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size). This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after any restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been -- expect this to fire alongside KvstoreCrashLooping rather than independently of it. Measured at the storage boundary so the cost is attributed to the right layer instead of surfacing as unexplained end-to-end slowness. Set histogram buckets to span a small file through a degraded one; the prometheus_client defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate.

annotations.summary: Store file is projected to exceed 1GB within a week
annotations.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows, and cost per operation rises linearly with it on both paths -- every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites it. The window in which a crash can truncate the dataset widens with it too. A projection rather than a threshold on current size, because this is a slow burn where the useful signal is the trajectory: a week of warning is enough to add compaction or migrate off the flat file, whereas discovering it at the limit is not. CALIBRATE 1e9 to the volume size and to the latency this deployment tolerates.

event.text: Adding the conditional conflict alert from phase 3's `mr-storage-write-conflicts`, so that failure mode has a direct detector rather than only the indirect key-count one.

annotations.summary: A concurrent modification of the backing file was detected during a write
annotations.description: CONDITIONAL -- deploy this only after confirming the deployment's concurrency model, the open question carried from phase 2 and still unresolved. Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file: two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish silently discards every key the first added, and both report success. If the out-of-repo sync job is single-threaded and the only writer, this mode is unreachable and both the metric and this alert should be dropped rather than built. If concurrent writers are possible, note the metric cannot be added on its own -- it requires first implementing the detection it counts (fcntl.flock, or comparing the file's mtime and size across the read-modify-write). KvstoreStoredKeyCountDropped catches the consequence of a lost update indirectly; this catches the race itself.

event.text:
Phase 4 accepted. 21 alert rules. All 24 non-excluded failure modes are mapped; nothing went silently unmapped.

**Coverage check**

|---|---|
| stale-read-served | cache-entries-outlive-ttl |
| negative-cache-poisoning | not-found-rate-elevated, negative-cache-entries-high |
| process-oom-crash | cache-entries-unbounded → memory-near-limit → crash-looping |
| read-storage-error-to-client | read-error-ratio |
| wrong-value-returned | invalid-records-detected |
| storage-data-loss | stored-key-count-dropped, not-found-rate-elevated |
| read-latency-degradation | read-latency-high |
| evictor-never-evicts | cache-entries-outlive-ttl, eviction-removing-nothing |
| evictor-not-scheduled | eviction-pass-not-running |
| write-path-no-invalidation | writes-not-invalidating |
| cache-unbounded-growth | cache-entries-unbounded |
| cache-caches-misses | negative-cache-entries-high |
| filesystem-read-failure | read-error-ratio, storage-read-errors |

| storage-torn-read | storage-read-errors |

**Deploy `KvstoreMetricsNotScraped` first.** It is the only rule that works today and the only one that can tell you the others are dead. Note the `absent(up{...})` arm — a target that never appeared produces no `up` series to compare against zero, so the obvious `up == 0` alone would never fire in exactly the case this service is in.

**Three things about this rule set worth flagging:**

**`KvstoreWritesNotInvalidatingCache` will fire immediately on current code and stay firing.** That is intended, not a misconfiguration — it is the missing `cache.evict` call in `admin.py` stated as an alert. It should be silenced only by fixing the code.

**`KvstoreStoredKeyCountDropped` is unusually precise.** The store has no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing *by construction* and any decrease is data loss with no benign explanation to triage past. It is also the only detector for a lost or misconfigured file path, since `Storage.get` returns `None` rather than raising when the file is absent.

**Two alerts deliberately catch the same bug from different sides.** `cache-entries-outlive-ttl` asserts the invariant (entries past TTL exist); `eviction-removing-nothing` asserts the mechanism (passes run, evict nothing). The first survives a fix and guards against regression; the second tells you *which* evictor fault you have — code bug versus dead scheduler — which the service currently cannot distinguish at all.

**Thresholds I could not derive from the code**, all marked CALIBRATE in the annotations: cache entry count (needs the memory limit and entry size), eviction interval, sync-job cadence, normal miss rate, and file-size ceiling. These are placeholders — deploying them unexamined would produce either noise or silence.

**One open question remains unresolved**, carried since phase 2: whether concurrent writers exist. `KvstoreWriteConflictsDetected` is marked conditional. If the sync job is single-threaded, that failure mode is unreachable and both the alert and its metric should be dropped rather than built — worth answering before implementing, since guessing wrong is costly in both directions.
before we wrap up -- can you revise the system map now that we've seen the rest of the analysis?

Yes — one genuine gap, and it's an inconsistency in my own map rather than a detail.

Phase 2 established `fm-evictor-not-scheduled` as a distinct failure mode from `fm-evictor-never-evicts`, with a different fix (deployment vs. code) and its own alert. But my map folded the out-of-repo scheduler into the evictor's description, while giving the out-of-repo *write* driver its own component (`sm-job-data-sync`). Both are unobservable external drivers of an in-repo function; only one got modelled. That asymmetry means the map doesn't show a dependency that phase 4 alerts on.

payload_or_id.description: The periodic loop that invokes kvstore/evictor.py:run_eviction_pass, referred to in that module's docstring as 'a caller (e.g. a scheduler loop)'. payload_or_id.name: Background cache eviction pass
payload_or_id.description: kvstore/evictor.py:run_eviction_pass(cache) -- the only mechanism that bounds cache growth, and the only mechanism that would ever correct a stale cache entry. Walks Cache.items(), collects keys whose age exceeds TTL_SECONDS (300s), evicts them, and returns the count so a caller can observe progress; nothing records that return value. Invoked by sm-job-eviction-scheduler, which is outside this repo. The comparison is unit-mismatched: `now` is epoch seconds while Entry.inserted_at_ms is epoch milliseconds, so `now - inserted_at_ms` is always a large negative number, the expiry condition is never true, and the pass evicts nothing. event.text:
Amendment applied and closed. Three edits to the system map.

**What changed**

1. **Added `sm-job-eviction-scheduler`** — the out-of-repo loop that calls `run_eviction_pass`, now a component in its own right with `sm-job-evictor` as its dependency.
2. **Updated `sm-job-evictor`** — references the scheduler, and now states explicitly that the unit-mismatched TTL check is the shared root of two independent critical chains, which phase 1 recorded as a single-component defect.
3. **Updated `sm-dep-prometheus-client`** — records the phase 3 grep as *verified* rather than suspected: one metric definition site, no exposition path of any kind.

**Why only these three.** The revision worth making was a genuine inconsistency, not a rewrite. My original map gave the out-of-repo *write* driver its own component (`sm-job-data-sync`) but folded the out-of-repo *eviction* driver into a description — two structurally identical external callers, modelled differently. Phase 2 then treated "the pass is broken" and "the pass is never called" as separate failure modes with separate fixes, and phase 4 wrote separate alerts for them, so the map was the only artifact not reflecting that split.

**One edit I considered and rejected.** Adding an `sm-entrypoint-admin-update-value → sm-service-cache` dependency edge. The write path *takes* a `Cache` parameter, so the edge is tempting — but it never calls it, so at runtime the dependency does not exist. The map states what is, and drawing the edge the code was designed to have would render the system as correct in the one diagram someone would consult to check. That gap stays visible where it belongs: `fm-write-path-no-invalidation`, alerted by `ar-writes-not-invalidating`. If the invalidation is ever wired up, that edge should be added in the same change.

**No downstream phases needed revising** — the new component is the origin of `fm-evictor-not-scheduled`, which was already documented, already classified as a metric gap against `mr-eviction-pass-liveness`, and already alerted. The analysis was right; the map just wasn't showing all of it.

The run is complete: 9 components, 28 failure modes, 1 implemented metric, 17 metric recommendations, 21 alert rules, 4 reasoned exclusions. Two open questions remain for you rather than for me — the writer concurrency model, and the five CALIBRATE thresholds that need deployment facts the code cannot supply.

Repair needed in phase 3: empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-expose-metrics-endpoint); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-cache-entries); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-cache-negative-entries); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-cache-lookups-total); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-cache-oldest-entry-age); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-eviction-pass-liveness); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-evicted-keys-total); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-cache-invalidations-total); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-storage-operations-total); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-storage-operation-duration); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-last-successful-write-timestamp); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-storage-size-and-keys); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-storage-invalid-records); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-filesystem-free-bytes); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-process-memory-and-restarts); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-storage-write-conflicts); empty_linkage_metric_recommendation (mr-get-value-found-label). Propose edits via propose_edits tagged for these phase(s), then call run_control with amend_complete when the repair is done.

payload_or_id.title: Wire a /metrics exposition endpoint and verify it is scraped
payload_or_id.description: No exposition path exists anywhere in this repo (verified by grep: no start_http_server, make_wsgi_app, generate_latest, or /metrics handler). Until this is wired, all instrumentation increments into a registry nobody reads.
payload_or_id.details: Call prometheus_client.start_http_server(port) at process start, or mount make_wsgi_app() in the serving application. Then verify by scraping the endpoint by hand and confirming the target appears UP in Prometheus -- never infer exposition from the code alone. This is a prerequisite for every other recommendation in this phase rather than a peer of them: an alert rule over a series that is never scraped does not fail loudly, it silently never fires, so the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind.
payload_or_id.rationale: Enabling exposition also brings prometheus_client's default process collectors at no extra code cost, which is what makes the OOM chain detectable.

event.text: `failure_mode_ids` accepted. Applying to the remaining 16 with full payloads.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_entries
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of current cache entry count
payload_or_id.description: Number of entries currently resident in Cache._entries.
payload_or_id.details: Set the gauge to len(self._entries) after each insertion in Cache.get and each removal in Cache.evict, or register it as a callback gauge so the value is computed at scrape time (cheaper and impossible to drift from reality). This is the single highest-value new metric in the analysis: it converts the OOM chain from undetectable-until-the-kill into a trend with hours or days of lead time, and because the count only ever rises while eviction is broken, a monotonic climb across a scrape window is direct evidence that no eviction is happening regardless of which of the two evictor faults is responsible.
payload_or_id.rationale: Detects the precursor rather than the outage. Memory-based detection alone would fire far later and would not distinguish cache growth from any other leak.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_negative_entries
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of cached entries holding a None value
payload_or_id.description: Count of resident entries whose value is None -- i.e. cached misses.
payload_or_id.details: Maintain alongside mr-cache-entries, or expose as a callback gauge counting entries with value is None. A rising negative count is the signature of miss-driven cache inflation (a scanner or a key-space probe) as distinct from legitimate working-set growth, and a persistently non-zero count is the population of keys at risk of being permanently pinned to None if the sync job later writes them.
payload_or_id.rationale: Separates the two causes of cache growth, which need different responses: legitimate growth calls for a capacity bound, miss-driven inflation calls for rate limiting or refusing to cache negatives.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_lookups_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of cache lookups labeled hit or miss
payload_or_id.description: Counts every Cache.get call, labeled result=hit|miss.
payload_or_id.details: Increment result="hit" on the early-return branch at cache.py:33 and result="miss" on the read-through branch at cache.py:34-36. The miss rate is the load actually reaching storage, which is what drives the linear-scan cost, and a step change in miss rate is the signature of a post-restart stampede. It also supplies the context the existing request counter lacks: a flat error rate means something very different depending on whether reads are reaching storage at all.
payload_or_id.rationale: Without this, a healthy-looking error rate cannot be distinguished from a cache so warm that storage is never exercised -- the storage backend could be entirely broken and invisible.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_oldest_entry_age_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of the age of the oldest resident cache entry
payload_or_id.description: Age in seconds of the oldest entry currently in the cache.
payload_or_id.details: Expose as a callback gauge computing now - min(inserted_at) over resident entries, taking care to divide by 1000 since inserted_at_ms is in milliseconds -- the same unit trap that produced fm-evictor-never-evicts. An entry older than TTL_SECONDS is by definition one the evictor should have removed, so this gauge exceeding 300s is direct proof that eviction is not working, and it proves it without needing to know whether the pass ran and found nothing or never ran at all.
payload_or_id.rationale: This is the most direct possible statement of the invariant the evictor exists to maintain. Unlike eviction counts, it cannot be satisfied by a pass that runs busily and removes the wrong things, and it stays meaningful after the unit bug is fixed.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_eviction_last_success_timestamp_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Counter of eviction passes plus last-completion timestamp gauge
payload_or_id.description: A kvstore_eviction_passes_total counter incremented on every completed pass, and a kvstore_eviction_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge set to the wall-clock time each pass completes.
payload_or_id.details: Instrument at the end of run_eviction_pass. The timestamp gauge is what makes 'the scheduler stopped calling this' detectable: a stalled pass leaves the gauge frozen while every other series in the system continues to look healthy. Note that the counter alone is insufficient -- alerting on rate(passes_total) == 0 fails to fire when the series stops being reported entirely, whereas time() minus the timestamp gauge keeps rising and crosses any threshold. The scheduler that drives this pass is modelled as sm-job-eviction-scheduler and lives outside the repo.
payload_or_id.rationale: Phase 2 established that a pass returning 0 and a pass that never ran produce identical evidence today. This separates them, which matters because they need different fixes: one is a code bug, the other a deployment fault.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_evicted_keys_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of keys removed by eviction
payload_or_id.description: Total keys evicted, incremented by the return value of run_eviction_pass.
payload_or_id.details: The function already computes exactly this number and its docstring states the purpose is so a caller can observe progress -- nothing records it. Increment by len(expired_keys) before returning. Pair with mr-eviction-pass-liveness: passes running while this counter stays flat is the precise signature of the seconds/milliseconds unit bug, and is what distinguishes it from the scheduler having stopped.
payload_or_id.rationale: Zero-cost to add since the value is already computed, and it is the one signal that would have made the existing unit-mismatch bug visible the day it shipped.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_invalidations_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of cache invalidations labeled by source
payload_or_id.description: Counts Cache.evict calls, labeled source=writer|evictor.
payload_or_id.details: Increment in Cache.evict with a source label supplied by the caller. Writes proceeding while source="writer" invalidations stay at zero is a direct, machine-checkable statement of fm-write-path-no-invalidation -- it detects the missing wiring itself rather than waiting for a user to observe stale data. This depends on mr-storage-operations-total to supply the write count for comparison.
payload_or_id.rationale: Catches the defect at the earliest link in the staleness chain. It also guards the fix: if someone later refactors update_value and drops the invalidation again, the ratio breaks immediately.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_operations_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of storage operations labeled by operation and outcome
payload_or_id.description: Counts every Storage.get and Storage.put, labeled operation=get|put and outcome=success|error.
payload_or_id.details: Instrument inside Storage.get and Storage.put, incrementing outcome="error" in the except OSError branches before raising StorageError. This is the single recommendation that lights up the entire write path, which today emits nothing at all: write volume, write failures, and by absence the liveness of the out-of-repo sync job all become visible. It also separates read-side from write-side storage failure, which the existing api.py counter conflates by only ever seeing the read side.
payload_or_id.rationale: The write path is the origin of every staleness and data-loss chain in this analysis and is currently 100% unobservable. Placing the counter in Storage rather than in admin.py means it cannot be bypassed by a future second writer.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_operation_duration_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Histogram of storage operation latency
payload_or_id.description: Latency distribution of Storage.get and Storage.put, labeled by operation.
payload_or_id.details: Wrap both method bodies with a Histogram timer. Since get() cost is O(file size) and put() reads and rewrites the whole file, this is the metric that turns the structural linear-scan cost into an observable trend and lets a threshold be set on user-facing miss latency rather than on the file size that proxies it. Use buckets that span the expected range from a small file to a degraded one; the prometheus_client defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate.
payload_or_id.rationale: There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service today, so read slowness has no signal at all. Measuring at the storage boundary attributes it to the right layer rather than leaving it as unexplained end-to-end slowness.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_last_successful_write_timestamp_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of the time of the last successful write
payload_or_id.description: Wall-clock timestamp of the most recent successful Storage.put.
payload_or_id.details: Set at the end of the successful path in Storage.put. Alerting on time() minus this gauge is the only way to detect that the out-of-repo sync job has stopped: with no write-side signal the service serves indefinitely frozen data while every component reports healthy. A timestamp gauge is used rather than rate() on a counter because it keeps producing a rising, alertable value even when writes cease entirely.
payload_or_id.rationale: Detects an upstream dependency failure from inside the service, without requiring access to the sync job's own instrumentation, which is out of this repo's control.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_keys
payload_or_id.title: Gauges of stored key count and backing file size
payload_or_id.description: kvstore_storage_keys (number of records in the store) and kvstore_storage_file_bytes (size of the backing file).
payload_or_id.details: Set both at the end of Storage.put, where the full record dict and the serialized payload are already in hand, so neither costs an extra file read. The key count is the only mechanism in this entire analysis capable of detecting fm-storage-data-loss: a truncating write, a torn rewrite, or a lost-update collision all manifest as the count dropping, and since the store has no delete operation, any decrease at all is by definition data loss. The byte gauge drives the growth and latency chains.
payload_or_id.rationale: Data loss is otherwise completely silent -- vanished keys return None with outcome="success", indistinguishable from keys that never existed. A monotonicity invariant on key count is the cheapest way to make it observable.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_invalid_records_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of records rejected or detected as unparseable
payload_or_id.description: Counts keys or values that violate the storage format, labeled reason=key_contains_delimiter|value_contains_newline|unparseable_line.
payload_or_id.details: This recommendation requires a small code change to be meaningful: Storage.put currently accepts any key or value without validation, so there is nothing to count. Add a guard rejecting keys containing a comma and values containing a newline, increment this counter with the reason, and raise rather than silently corrupting the file. Also increment reason="unparseable_line" in get() for any line that fails to partition cleanly, which catches pre-existing corruption on read.
payload_or_id.rationale: Silent corruption is the worst class of failure here because the client receives a well-formed value belonging to a different key and every layer reports success. Converting it into a loud rejection at write time is preferable to detecting it after the fact; the counter exists to prove the guard is holding and to size any pre-existing damage.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_filesystem_free_bytes
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of free space on the volume holding the store
payload_or_id.description: Free bytes on the filesystem containing the storage path.
payload_or_id.details: Expose as a callback gauge using shutil.disk_usage(self._path.parent).free. Check first whether node_exporter or an equivalent already covers this volume -- if it does, prefer that series and skip this recommendation rather than duplicating it, since the node-level metric is better maintained and covers volumes this process never touches. Add it in-process only if the store lives somewhere the node exporter does not observe, or if the deployment has no node-level monitoring.
payload_or_id.rationale: ENOSPC is unusually dangerous here because put() rewrites the whole file: a full disk does not merely reject the write, it truncates the dataset. Free space needs headroom of roughly one full file size, which is a stricter condition than a generic disk alert would use.

payload_or_id.name: process_resident_memory_bytes
payload_or_id.title: Enable default process collectors for memory and restart detection
payload_or_id.description: process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds, supplied automatically by prometheus_client's default collectors.
payload_or_id.details: These require no instrumentation code -- prometheus_client registers them with the default registry automatically, so they arrive as soon as mr-expose-metrics-endpoint is done. Resident memory approaching the container limit is the last-line signal for the OOM chain, and a change in process_start_time_seconds detects the restart after a kill has already happened. Treat both as backstops behind mr-cache-entries, which fires far earlier.
payload_or_id.rationale: Listed explicitly despite being free because it would otherwise be assumed present. Memory alone is a poor primary signal here: it fires late and does not attribute the growth to the cache, but it does catch leaks the cache gauge would miss.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_write_conflicts_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of detected concurrent-write conflicts (conditional)
payload_or_id.description: Counts writes that detected a competing modification of the backing file.
payload_or_id.details: CONDITIONAL -- confirm the deployment's concurrency model before implementing. If the out-of-repo sync job is single-threaded and is the only writer, fm-concurrent-write-lost-update is unreachable and this metric should be dropped rather than built. If concurrent writers are possible, the metric cannot be implemented alone: it requires first adding the conflict detection it counts (an advisory lock via fcntl.flock, or comparing the file's mtime and size between the read and the write inside put()). Increment when a competing modification is observed.
payload_or_id.rationale: Recorded as an open question rather than resolved either way, because the code cannot answer it and guessing wrong is costly in both directions -- building unnecessary locking, or leaving a silent data-loss path unmonitored.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_get_value_requests_total
payload_or_id.title: Add a found label to the existing request counter
payload_or_id.description: Extend the existing kvstore_get_value_requests_total with a second label, found=true|false, distinguishing reads that returned a value from reads that returned None.
payload_or_id.details: Change to the existing metric defined at kvstore/api.py:19-23: add "found" to the label list and set it from whether the returned value is None at the two increment sites. Cardinality cost is one extra dimension of two values, which is negligible. Today a read returning None and a read returning a value are both counted identically as outcome="success", so the service cannot distinguish serving data from serving nothing. A sustained rise in found="false" is the client-side signature of both negative-cache poisoning and mass data loss.
payload_or_id.rationale: The cheapest change in this phase and the only one to an existing metric. It does not by itself prove which of the two causes is responsible -- that needs mr-storage-size-and-keys and mr-cache-negative-entries -- but it is the signal that says something is wrong from the user's point of view, which the current counter cannot express at all.
