payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_lookups_total
payload_or_id.title: Counter of cache lookups labeled hit or miss
payload_or_id.description: Counts every Cache.get call, labeled result=hit|miss.
payload_or_id.details: Increment result="hit" on the early-return branch at cache.py:33 and result="miss" on the read-through branch at cache.py:34-36. The miss rate is the load actually reaching storage, which is what drives the linear-scan cost. It also supplies the context the existing request counter lacks: a flat error rate means something very different depending on whether reads are reaching storage at all. Note this metric also makes a post-restart read-through stampede visible as a step change in miss rate, but fm-cache-cleared-on-restart is deliberately NOT listed as a served failure mode -- it is an excluded mode, and its consequences are covered via fm-read-latency-degradation.
payload_or_id.rationale: Without this, a healthy-looking error rate cannot be distinguished from a cache so warm that storage is never exercised -- the storage backend could be entirely broken and invisible.

payload_or_id.name: process_resident_memory_bytes
payload_or_id.title: Enable default process collectors for memory and restart detection
payload_or_id.description: process_resident_memory_bytes and process_start_time_seconds, supplied automatically by prometheus_client's default collectors.
payload_or_id.details: These require no instrumentation code -- prometheus_client registers them with the default registry automatically, so they arrive as soon as mr-expose-metrics-endpoint is done. Resident memory approaching the container limit is the last-line signal for the OOM chain, and repeated changes in process_start_time_seconds detect the crash-loop sawtooth after a kill has already happened. Treat both as backstops behind mr-cache-entries, which fires far earlier. Restart visibility is a by-product here; fm-cache-cleared-on-restart is excluded and is deliberately not claimed as a served failure mode, since routine restarts are expected and are not a condition to alert on.
payload_or_id.rationale: Listed explicitly despite being free because it would otherwise be assumed present. Memory alone is a poor primary signal here: it fires late and does not attribute the growth to the cache, but it does catch leaks the cache gauge would miss.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_storage_operation_duration_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Histogram of storage operation latency
payload_or_id.description: Latency distribution of Storage.get and Storage.put, labeled by operation.
payload_or_id.details: Wrap both method bodies with a Histogram timer. Since get() cost is O(file size) and put() reads and rewrites the whole file, this turns the structural cost of the linear scan into an observable trend and lets a threshold be set on user-facing miss latency rather than on the file size that proxies it. Use buckets that span the expected range from a small file to a degraded one; the prometheus_client defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate. fm-storage-linear-scan is excluded and is deliberately not claimed as a served failure mode: the scan is the intended algorithm and is unconditionally true, so this histogram measures its varying consequence rather than detecting the scan itself.
payload_or_id.rationale: There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service today, so read slowness has no signal at all. Measuring at the storage boundary attributes it to the right layer rather than leaving it as unexplained end-to-end slowness.

annotations.summary: kvstore metrics target is down or has never been scraped
annotations.description: Prometheus cannot scrape kvstore. This alert must exist before any other rule here is trusted: the service defines its Counter but wires no exposition endpoint, so if start_http_server or make_wsgi_app was never called, every other alert in this group evaluates over a non-existent series and silently never fires -- the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. The absent() arm is the load-bearing half: a target that never appeared at all produces no up series to compare against zero. Verify by scraping the endpoint by hand; never infer exposition from the code.

payload_or_id.name: KvstoreInstrumentationMissing
payload_or_id.expr:
absent(kvstore_cache_entries)
or absent(kvstore_cache_lookups_total)
or absent(kvstore_evicted_keys_total)
or absent(kvstore_eviction_last_success_timestamp_seconds)
or absent(kvstore_storage_operations_total)
or absent(kvstore_last_successful_write_timestamp_seconds)

annotations.summary: One or more kvstore instrumentation series has stopped being reported
annotations.description: A metric added to close a phase-3 gap is no longer present. This is the dead-man's switch for the instrumentation itself: the cache, evictor, and write path each emitted nothing at all before this work, and a refactor that drops a Gauge or moves a counter out of the code path would silently return them to that state -- with every alert built on them going quiet rather than red. Enable only after the corresponding metrics ship, or it fires immediately. Treat a firing instance as 'the alerts you think you have are gone', not as a metrics-plumbing nuisance.

annotations.summary: Over 1% of get_value calls are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: Clients are receiving errors from the read path. This is the only alert in the group that needs no new instrumentation -- it runs against the counter already defined at kvstore/api.py:19-23. Expressed as a ratio rather than an absolute rate deliberately: cache hits never reach storage, so a completely unreadable backing file presents as a partial failure whose apparent size depends on cache warmth, and an absolute threshold would be calibrated to traffic that may not be reaching storage at all. The trailing rate>0 guard prevents a division-by-zero NaN from suppressing the alert during idle periods. Expect the ratio to jump after any restart, when every read is a miss.

annotations.summary: The storage layer is failing to read the backing file
annotations.description: Storage.get raised OSError -- permission change, I/O error, unmounted volume, exhausted file descriptors -- or read the file while a rewrite was in flight. Fires at the storage boundary rather than at the entrypoint, so it detects the fault even when a warm cache is absorbing most reads and the client-facing error ratio stays below its threshold. Any non-zero count is worth investigating: this path should never fail in normal operation. Note what this does NOT catch: a missing or misconfigured file path, because Storage.get returns None rather than raising when the file is absent -- that variant is covered by KvstoreStoredKeyCountDropped.

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is large and still rising with no sign of eviction
annotations.description: The cache is growing monotonically toward an OOM kill. This is the earliest actionable point in the memory chain and the reason to alert here rather than on memory: it gives hours to days of lead time, and it attributes the growth to the cache rather than to an unspecified leak. The two conditions are both needed -- absolute size alone fires on a legitimately large working set, and positive derivative alone fires on ordinary warm-up. CALIBRATE the 500000 threshold against the container memory limit divided by average entry size before enabling; the value here is a placeholder, not a measurement. Growth is driven by the unique-key rate, not the request rate, so a scan or a crawler moves this far faster than traffic volume suggests.

annotations.summary: kvstore resident memory is within 15% of its limit
annotations.description: The process is approaching an OOM kill, which takes the service down entirely and fails every in-flight request. This is the last-line backstop behind KvstoreCacheEntriesGrowingUnbounded, which fires far earlier -- by the time this one is up there may be minutes rather than hours. Comes free from prometheus_client's default collectors once exposition is wired. If cAdvisor is not present in this deployment, replace the denominator with the literal limit in bytes rather than dropping the alert.

annotations.summary: kvstore has restarted more than three times in six hours
annotations.description: Repeated restarts are the signature of the OOM sawtooth this design produces: the cache fills, the process is killed, it restarts with an empty cache, and the climb begins again on an interval set only by traffic mix. Thresholded at more than three restarts specifically so a routine deploy does not page -- a single restart is expected and is deliberately not alerted on. Each restart also drops the entire cache, so every one of them is followed immediately by the worst-case cold-cache latency window; expect KvstoreReadLatencyHigh to fire alongside this.

annotations.summary: Cached entries are older than twice the configured TTL
annotations.description: An entry older than TTL_SECONDS (300) is by definition one the evictor should have removed, so this asserts the exact invariant the evictor exists to maintain. It is the primary detector for the seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch in evictor.py, and it detects that fault without needing to know whether the pass ran and found nothing or never ran at all. It is also the closest available proxy for stale reads, which are otherwise entirely undetectable -- every stale read is counted as outcome=success, so no rule over the existing counter can find them at any threshold. Because the same broken TTL check is the only bound on cache size AND the only mechanism that corrects a stale entry, this one alert covers the root of two separate critical chains.

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are running but removing no entries while expired ones exist
annotations.description: The precise signature of the unit-mismatch bug: the scheduler is calling run_eviction_pass, the pass completes, and yet nothing is evicted despite entries being past TTL. All three conditions are required -- without the passes term this also fires when the scheduler has stopped (a different fault with a different fix, covered by KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning), and without the age term it fires harmlessly whenever there is genuinely nothing to evict. Diagnostic value beyond detection: this distinguishes 'the code is wrong' from 'the job is not running', which the service today cannot tell apart at all.

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has completed in 15 minutes
annotations.description: The scheduler loop that drives run_eviction_pass (sm-job-eviction-scheduler) lives outside this repo, so it can be missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged with nothing in the service noticing. Written against a last-completion timestamp rather than rate() over a counter for a specific reason: when a job stops entirely its counter stops changing, and a rate-based rule goes quiet rather than firing, whereas time() minus a frozen timestamp keeps rising and crosses any threshold. CALIBRATE the 900s against the scheduler's actual interval (roughly three missed runs is a reasonable starting point); that interval is not knowable from this repo.

annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache invalidation is following them
annotations.description: States the defect in admin.update_value directly: it takes a Cache parameter and never calls cache.evict, so a key already resident keeps serving its pre-write value. Detecting the missing wiring is far better than waiting for a user to notice stale data, which is the only way this surfaces today. This alert will fire immediately on the current code and should stay firing until the invalidation is wired up -- that is the intended behaviour, not a misconfiguration. Once fixed it becomes a regression guard: if a later refactor drops the evict call again, the ratio breaks the same way.

annotations.summary: No successful write to storage in six hours
annotations.description: The periodic data-sync job is the only writer in the system. If it stops, crashes, or is descheduled, storage quietly freezes at its last state and the service serves indefinitely old data while every component reports healthy -- reads keep succeeding, error rates stay flat, and nothing anywhere goes red. This detects an out-of-repo dependency failure from inside the service, without needing access to that job's own instrumentation. CALIBRATE 21600s against the sync job's actual cadence, which is not knowable from this repo -- flagged as an open question in phase 3 and still open.

annotations.summary: Storage writes are failing
annotations.description: Storage.put raised OSError -- most likely a full disk, a permissions change, or an unwritable parent directory. Today this is completely silent inside the service: update_value lets StorageError propagate with no counter and no log, so whether anyone finds out depends entirely on the out-of-repo sync job's error handling, which this codebase does not control. Treat any occurrence as urgent despite the warning severity: because put() rewrites the whole file in place with no atomic replace, a write that fails partway does not merely reject the update, it can truncate the entire dataset.

annotations.summary: The number of keys in the store has decreased -- data has been lost
annotations.description: The store exposes no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and ANY decrease is by definition data loss. That makes this an unusually precise alert: there is no benign explanation to triage past. It is the only mechanism in this entire analysis capable of detecting a truncated or torn rewrite, a lost update from concurrent writers, or a backing file that has been replaced or lost -- all of which are otherwise perfectly silent, because vanished keys return None with outcome=success, indistinguishable from keys that never existed. Investigate immediately and expect to restore from backup; the service will not recover on its own.

annotations.summary: Free disk space is under twice the size of the store file
annotations.description: Thresholded against the store's own size rather than as a percentage of the volume, because that is what the failure actually depends on: Storage.put serialises the entire dataset and writes it in one call, so every single write needs free space of the order of the whole file. A generic 90%-full disk alert can therefore fire far too late on a large store, or far too early on a small one. ENOSPC here is not a rejected write -- the non-atomic rewrite turns a full disk directly into dataset-wide truncation. If node_exporter already covers this volume, prefer its series over adding an in-process gauge.

annotations.summary: A key or value violating the storage format was rejected or found in the store
annotations.description: The store's line format is unescaped key,value split on the first comma, with no validation. A key containing a comma reads back as a different key with a different value, and a value containing a newline writes a phantom record that can shadow a real key. The client then receives a well-formed value belonging to someone else, reported as outcome=success -- silent corruption with no signal at any layer. This is the one failure mode where instrumentation alone is not the answer: the counter only exists once write-time validation is added, and its real job is to prove that guard is holding and to size any corruption already in the file. reason="unparseable_line" indicates pre-existing damage found on read rather than a newly blocked write.

annotations.summary: Over 30% of successful reads are returning no value
annotations.description: The client-side symptom shared by negative-cache poisoning and mass data loss: clients are being told a key does not exist. Requires the found label added to the existing counter -- today a read returning None and a read returning data are counted identically, so the service cannot distinguish serving data from serving nothing. This alert says something is wrong from the user's point of view; it does not identify which cause. Disambiguate with kvstore_cache_negative_entries (poisoning) and kvstore_storage_keys (loss). CALIBRATE 0.3 against the normal miss rate for this key space, which may legitimately be high.

annotations.summary: Most of the cache is cached misses, which never expire
annotations.description: Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) on a miss and the cache has no working expiry, so every cached miss is permanent. Two consequences, both live here: any key read before the sync job first writes it is pinned to None forever and becomes invisible to every client, and an attacker or buggy client probing random keys can inflate the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain. A high and rising negative share is the signature that distinguishes miss-driven inflation from legitimate working-set growth -- which matters because they call for different fixes: rate limiting or refusing to cache negatives, versus a capacity bound.

annotations.summary: p99 storage read latency is above 500ms
annotations.description: Every cache miss reads the entire backing file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size). This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after any restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been -- expect this to fire alongside KvstoreCrashLooping rather than independently of it. Measured at the storage boundary so the cost is attributed to the right layer instead of surfacing as unexplained end-to-end slowness. Set histogram buckets to span a small file through a degraded one; the prometheus_client defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate.

annotations.summary: Store file is projected to exceed 1GB within a week
annotations.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows, and cost per operation rises linearly with it on both paths -- every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites it. The window in which a crash can truncate the dataset widens with it too. A projection rather than a threshold on current size, because this is a slow burn where the useful signal is the trajectory: a week of warning is enough to add compaction or migrate off the flat file, whereas discovering it at the limit is not. CALIBRATE 1e9 to the volume size and to the latency this deployment tolerates.

annotations.summary: A concurrent modification of the backing file was detected during a write
annotations.description: CONDITIONAL -- deploy this only after confirming the deployment's concurrency model, the open question carried from phase 2 and still unresolved. Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file: two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish silently discards every key the first added, and both report success. If the out-of-repo sync job is single-threaded and the only writer, this mode is unreachable and both the metric and this alert should be dropped rather than built. If concurrent writers are possible, note the metric cannot be added on its own -- it requires first implementing the detection it counts (fcntl.flock, or comparing the file's mtime and size across the read-modify-write). KvstoreStoredKeyCountDropped catches the consequence of a lost update indirectly; this catches the race itself.

event.text: Both batches accepted.

payload.summary: Repaired three defect classes, two of which shared one root cause. (1) empty_linkage_alert_recommendation on all 21 alerts: I again wrote the failure-mode linkage under 'serves_failure_modes' rather than 'failure_mode_ids' -- the same field-name error I had just repaired in metric-recommendations, repeated in phase 4 because I corrected the instance rather than checking every artifact that carried the same linkage. All 21 alerts re-sent as full-payload updates with 'failure_mode_ids'. (2) unmapped_failure_mode on all 24 non-excluded failure modes: not an independent defect but the downstream consequence of (1) -- with alert linkage unreadable, no failure mode had a detector. Resolved by the same fix; re-verified that each of the 24 appears in at least one alert's failure_mode_ids. (3) excluded_with_metric_coverage on fm-cache-cleared-on-restart and fm-storage-linear-scan: three recommendations (mr-cache-lookups-total, mr-process-memory-and-restarts, mr-storage-operation-duration) listed excluded failure modes as served. That was wrong -- an excluded mode has no detection by definition, and claiming coverage for one would have made the exclusions look contradicted. The other two exclusions (fm-cache-no-size-bound, fm-storage-nonatomic-rewrite) were already clean. annotations.description: Prometheus cannot scrape kvstore. This alert must exist before any other rule here is trusted: the service defines its Counter but wires no exposition endpoint, so if start_http_server or make_wsgi_app was never called, every other alert in this group evaluates over a non-existent series and silently never fires -- the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. The absent() arm is the load-bearing half: a target that never appeared at all produces no up series to compare against zero. annotations.summary: One or more kvstore instrumentation series has stopped being reported
annotations.description: A metric added to close a phase-3 gap is no longer present. This is the dead-man's switch for the instrumentation itself: the cache, evictor, and write path each emitted nothing at all before this work, and a refactor that drops a Gauge or moves a counter out of the code path would silently return them to that state -- with every alert built on them going quiet rather than red. Enable only after the corresponding metrics ship, or it fires immediately. Treat a firing instance as 'the alerts you think you have are gone', not as a metrics-plumbing nuisance.

annotations.summary: Over 1% of get_value calls are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: Clients are receiving errors from the read path. This is the only alert in the group that needs no new instrumentation -- it runs against the counter already defined at kvstore/api.py:19-23. Expressed as a ratio rather than an absolute rate deliberately: cache hits never reach storage, so a completely unreadable backing file presents as a partial failure whose apparent size depends on cache warmth, and an absolute threshold would be calibrated to traffic that may not be reaching storage at all. The trailing rate>0 guard prevents a division-by-zero NaN from suppressing the alert during idle periods. Expect the ratio to jump after any restart, when every read is a miss.

annotations.summary: The storage layer is failing to read the backing file
annotations.description: Storage.get raised OSError -- permission change, I/O error, unmounted volume, exhausted file descriptors -- or read the file while a rewrite was in flight. Fires at the storage boundary rather than at the entrypoint, so it detects the fault even when a warm cache is absorbing most reads and the client-facing error ratio stays below its threshold. Any non-zero count is worth investigating: this path should never fail in normal operation. Note what this does NOT catch: a missing or misconfigured file path, because Storage.get returns None rather than raising when the file is absent -- that variant is covered by KvstoreStoredKeyCountDropped.

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is large and still rising with no sign of eviction
annotations.description: The cache is growing monotonically toward an OOM kill. This is the earliest actionable point in the memory chain and the reason to alert here rather than on memory: it gives hours to days of lead time, and it attributes the growth to the cache rather than to an unspecified leak. The two conditions are both needed -- absolute size alone fires on a legitimately large working set, and positive derivative alone fires on ordinary warm-up. CALIBRATE the 500000 threshold against the container memory limit divided by average entry size before enabling; the value here is a placeholder, not a measurement. Growth is driven by the unique-key rate, not the request rate, so a scan or a crawler moves this far faster than traffic volume suggests.

annotations.summary: kvstore resident memory is within 15% of its limit
annotations.description: The process is approaching an OOM kill, which takes the service down entirely and fails every in-flight request. This is the last-line backstop behind KvstoreCacheEntriesGrowingUnbounded, which fires far earlier -- by the time this one is up there may be minutes rather than hours. Comes free from prometheus_client's default collectors once exposition is wired. If cAdvisor is not present in this deployment, replace the denominator with the literal limit in bytes rather than dropping the alert.

annotations.summary: kvstore has restarted more than three times in six hours
annotations.description: Repeated restarts are the signature of the OOM sawtooth this design produces: the cache fills, the process is killed, it restarts with an empty cache, and the climb begins again on an interval set only by traffic mix. Thresholded at more than three restarts specifically so a routine deploy does not page -- a single restart is expected and is deliberately not alerted on. Each restart also drops the entire cache, so every one of them is followed immediately by the worst-case cold-cache latency window; expect KvstoreReadLatencyHigh to fire alongside this.

annotations.summary: Cached entries are older than twice the configured TTL
annotations.description: An entry older than TTL_SECONDS (300) is by definition one the evictor should have removed, so this asserts the exact invariant the evictor exists to maintain. It is the primary detector for the seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch in evictor.py, and it detects that fault without needing to know whether the pass ran and found nothing or never ran at all. It is also the closest available proxy for stale reads, which are otherwise entirely undetectable -- every stale read is counted as outcome=success, so no rule over the existing counter can find them at any threshold. Because the same broken TTL check is the only bound on cache size AND the only mechanism that corrects a stale entry, this one alert covers the root of two separate critical chains.

annotations.summary: Eviction passes are running but removing no entries while expired ones exist
annotations.description: The precise signature of the unit-mismatch bug: the scheduler is calling run_eviction_pass, the pass completes, and yet nothing is evicted despite entries being past TTL. All three conditions are required -- without the passes term this also fires when the scheduler has stopped (a different fault with a different fix, covered by KvstoreEvictionPassNotRunning), and without the age term it fires harmlessly whenever there is genuinely nothing to evict. Diagnostic value beyond detection: this distinguishes 'the code is wrong' from 'the job is not running', which the service today cannot tell apart at all.

annotations.summary: No eviction pass has completed in 15 minutes
annotations.description: The scheduler loop that drives run_eviction_pass (sm-job-eviction-scheduler) lives outside this repo, so it can be missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged with nothing in the service noticing. Written against a last-completion timestamp rather than rate() over a counter for a specific reason: when a job stops entirely its counter stops changing, and a rate-based rule goes quiet rather than firing, whereas time() minus a frozen timestamp keeps rising and crosses any threshold. CALIBRATE the 900s against the scheduler's actual interval (roughly three missed runs is a reasonable starting point); that interval is not knowable from this repo.

annotations.summary: Writes are succeeding but no cache invalidation is following them
annotations.description: States the defect in admin.update_value directly: it takes a Cache parameter and never calls cache.evict, so a key already resident keeps serving its pre-write value. Detecting the missing wiring is far better than waiting for a user to notice stale data, which is the only way this surfaces today. This alert will fire immediately on the current code and should stay firing until the invalidation is wired up -- that is the intended behaviour, not a misconfiguration. Once fixed it becomes a regression guard: if a later refactor drops the evict call again, the ratio breaks the same way.

annotations.summary: No successful write to storage in six hours
annotations.description: The periodic data-sync job is the only writer in the system. If it stops, crashes, or is descheduled, storage quietly freezes at its last state and the service serves indefinitely old data while every component reports healthy -- reads keep succeeding, error rates stay flat, and nothing anywhere goes red. This detects an out-of-repo dependency failure from inside the service, without needing access to that job's own instrumentation. CALIBRATE 21600s against the sync job's actual cadence, which is not knowable from this repo -- flagged as an open question in phase 3 and still open.

annotations.summary: Storage writes are failing
annotations.description: Storage.put raised OSError -- most likely a full disk, a permissions change, or an unwritable parent directory. Today this is completely silent inside the service: update_value lets StorageError propagate with no counter and no log, so whether anyone finds out depends entirely on the out-of-repo sync job's error handling, which this codebase does not control. Treat any occurrence as urgent despite the warning severity: because put() rewrites the whole file in place with no atomic replace, a write that fails partway does not merely reject the update, it can truncate the entire dataset.

annotations.summary: The number of keys in the store has decreased -- data has been lost
annotations.description: The store exposes no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and ANY decrease is by definition data loss. That makes this an unusually precise alert: there is no benign explanation to triage past. It is the only mechanism in this entire analysis capable of detecting a truncated or torn rewrite, a lost update from concurrent writers, or a backing file that has been replaced or lost -- all of which are otherwise perfectly silent, because vanished keys return None with outcome=success, indistinguishable from keys that never existed. Investigate immediately and expect to restore from backup; the service will not recover on its own.

annotations.summary: Free disk space is under twice the size of the store file
annotations.description: Thresholded against the store's own size rather than as a percentage of the volume, because that is what the failure actually depends on: Storage.put serialises the entire dataset and writes it in one call, so every single write needs free space of the order of the whole file. A generic 90%-full disk alert can therefore fire far too late on a large store, or far too early on a small one. ENOSPC here is not a rejected write -- the non-atomic rewrite turns a full disk directly into dataset-wide truncation. If node_exporter already covers this volume, prefer its series over adding an in-process gauge.

annotations.summary: A key or value violating the storage format was rejected or found in the store
annotations.description: The store's line format is unescaped key,value split on the first comma, with no validation. A key containing a comma reads back as a different key with a different value, and a value containing a newline writes a phantom record that can shadow a real key. The client then receives a well-formed value belonging to someone else, reported as outcome=success -- silent corruption with no signal at any layer. This is the one failure mode where instrumentation alone is not the answer: the counter only exists once write-time validation is added, and its real job is to prove that guard is holding and to size any corruption already in the file. reason="unparseable_line" indicates pre-existing damage found on read rather than a newly blocked write.

annotations.summary: Over 30% of successful reads are returning no value
annotations.description: The client-side symptom shared by negative-cache poisoning and mass data loss: clients are being told a key does not exist. Requires the found label added to the existing counter -- today a read returning None and a read returning data are counted identically, so the service cannot distinguish serving data from serving nothing. This alert says something is wrong from the user's point of view; it does not identify which cause. Disambiguate with kvstore_cache_negative_entries (poisoning) and kvstore_storage_keys (loss). CALIBRATE 0.3 against the normal miss rate for this key space, which may legitimately be high.

annotations.summary: Most of the cache is cached misses, which never expire
annotations.description: Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) on a miss and the cache has no working expiry, so every cached miss is permanent. Two consequences, both live here: any key read before the sync job first writes it is pinned to None forever and becomes invisible to every client, and an attacker or buggy client probing random keys can inflate the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain. A high and rising negative share is the signature that distinguishes miss-driven inflation from legitimate working-set growth -- which matters because they call for different fixes: rate limiting or refusing to cache negatives, versus a capacity bound.

annotations.summary: p99 storage read latency is above 500ms
annotations.description: Every cache miss reads the entire backing file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size). This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after any restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been -- expect this to fire alongside KvstoreCrashLooping rather than independently of it. Measured at the storage boundary so the cost is attributed to the right layer instead of surfacing as unexplained end-to-end slowness. Set histogram buckets to span a small file through a degraded one; the prometheus_client defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate.

annotations.summary: Store file is projected to exceed 1GB within a week
annotations.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows, and cost per operation rises linearly with it on both paths -- every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites it. The window in which a crash can truncate the dataset widens with it too. A projection rather than a threshold on current size, because this is a slow burn where the useful signal is the trajectory: a week of warning is enough to add compaction or migrate off the flat file, whereas discovering it at the limit is not. CALIBRATE 1e9 to the volume size and to the latency this deployment tolerates.

annotations.summary: A concurrent modification of the backing file was detected during a write
annotations.description: CONDITIONAL -- deploy this only after confirming the deployment's concurrency model, the open question carried from phase 2 and still unresolved. Storage.put is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file: two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish silently discards every key the first added, and both report success. If the out-of-repo sync job is single-threaded and the only writer, this mode is unreachable and both the metric and this alert should be dropped rather than built. If concurrent writers are possible, note the metric cannot be added on its own -- it requires first implementing the detection it counts (fcntl.flock, or comparing the file's mtime and size across the read-modify-write). KvstoreStoredKeyCountDropped catches the consequence of a lost update indirectly; this catches the race itself.

payload_or_id.rationale: kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} increments on exactly this failure; only an alert rule is missing. Caveat: because cache hits never reach storage, this counter under-reports a storage outage in proportion to cache warmth, so the rule triggers on error ratio against total requests rather than absolute rate.

Every OSError on read becomes a StorageError and is already counted as outcome="error", so this is detectable today with a rule alone. Limit of that coverage: it catches the file being present but unreadable, not the file being absent, because Storage.get returns None rather than raising -- that variant is covered under fm-storage-data-loss. ar-storage-read-errors separates read-side from write-side filesystem failure, which the entrypoint counter cannot do.

The existing counter reports outcome="success" for every stale read, so no rule over current instrumentation can detect this at any threshold. Detection moves upstream: ar-cache-entries-outlive-ttl proves entries are outliving the TTL. It does not observe staleness directly -- that would require comparing cached against stored values -- but it detects the mechanism that produces it.

Today a poisoned None and a legitimately absent key are byte-identical at the only instrumented point. ar-not-found-rate-elevated makes the user-visible symptom detectable; ar-negative-cache-entries-high sizes the at-risk population. Full certainty still requires correlating a found=false read against a key present in storage, which no single rule can express.

Nothing observes memory or entry count, so the first evidence today is the kill itself. ar-memory-near-limit is the late backstop and ar-crash-looping confirms the sawtooth after the fact; the precursor worth acting on is ar-cache-entries-unbounded under fm-cache-unbounded-growth, which fires hours to days earlier.

Corrupted values are well-formed strings returned as outcome="success"; no rule can detect that a returned value belongs to a different key. Covered by prevention plus a proof-of-guard alert rather than by detection: ar-invalid-records-detected requires write-time validation, which converts silent corruption into a loud rejection. Stated plainly because this is the one failure mode where alerting alone is not a sufficient answer.

Vanished keys return None with outcome="success", indistinguishable from keys that never existed. ar-stored-key-count-dropped is the only rule capable of detecting it: the store has no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and any drop is by definition data loss.

There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so slow reads produce no signal at all. ar-read-latency-high measures the user-facing symptom at the storage boundary; the miss-rate and file-size metrics explain it and are what make the alert actionable rather than merely true.

The evictor emits nothing, so a pass that removes zero entries forever is silent. ar-cache-entries-outlive-ttl asserts the invariant and survives the fix as a regression guard; ar-eviction-removing-nothing asserts the mechanism and distinguishes this code bug from a dead scheduler, which the service today cannot tell apart.

Not detectable today, and specifically not separable from fm-evictor-never-evicts. ar-eviction-pass-not-running resolves that using a last-completion timestamp, which keeps producing a rising alertable value when the pass stops entirely -- a rate() rule would go quiet instead of firing.

The write path emits nothing, so the missing invalidation is invisible until a user reads stale data. ar-writes-not-invalidating makes the defect itself machine-checkable -- writes occurring while writer-sourced invalidations stay at zero -- and will fire immediately against current code, which is intended.

No metric observes cache size. ar-cache-entries-unbounded is the earliest actionable point in the memory chain and the highest-value addition in the analysis, converting an outage with no warning into a trend with hours to days of lead time.

Not observable today. Kept as a gap rather than an exclusion because the count of resident None entries is a genuinely varying runtime quantity: it distinguishes an adversarial or buggy key-space probe from ordinary growth, and sizes the population at risk of permanent None-pinning.

Write-side OSError is entirely uninstrumented today, so a full disk is silent until it has already truncated the dataset. ar-storage-write-errors catches the failed write; ar-filesystem-low-headroom catches it beforehand, thresholded against the store's own size because put() needs free space of the order of the whole file on every write.

A torn read surfaces either as a StorageError, which ar-storage-read-errors catches, or as a silent None that gets cached and outlives the race. The silent variant remains undetected -- a residual gap worth stating rather than papering over.

OPEN QUESTION, still unresolved: whether concurrent writers exist depends on the out-of-repo sync job's threading model. If it is single-threaded and the only writer, this mode is unreachable and should be reclassified as excluded, dropping ar-write-conflicts-detected and its metric. ar-stored-key-count-dropped catches the consequence indirectly regardless.

Nothing validates keys or values on write, so malformed records enter the store silently and only surface as corruption on a later read. The alert requires that validation to be added first; it then proves the guard is holding and sizes any pre-existing damage found on read.

Neither file size nor key count is measured. ar-storage-file-growth alerts on the trajectory rather than the current value, because this is a slow burn where a week of warning is enough to add compaction and discovering it at the limit is not.

Self-referential: this cannot be detected by any metric the service emits, because its content is that emitted metrics do not arrive. Detection comes from the monitoring system's own view -- ar-metrics-not-scraped over target UP plus an absent() arm for a target that never appeared. Prerequisite for every other alert in the run.

This failure mode is the absence of instrumentation itself, so it is a gap by definition. ar-instrumentation-missing is the dead-man's switch that detects a regression back to that state -- a dropped counter makes every alert built on it go quiet rather than red.

StorageError from put() propagates into out-of-repo code with no counter, log, or trace inside the service. ar-storage-write-errors makes write failures visible from inside this service, which matters because whether the sync job reports its own errors is outside this codebase's control.

The cache emits nothing at all. Beyond enabling the growth and staleness chains, the hit/miss counter fixes a blind spot in the metric that does exist: a flat error rate cannot currently distinguish a healthy backend from a cache so warm that storage is never exercised.

The pass computes the eviction count expressly so a caller can observe progress, per its own docstring, and nothing records it. Recording it plus a completion timestamp is the minimum that makes the evictor's two failure modes distinguishable from each other and from healthy operation.

A frozen upstream job is invisible from inside the service today: no write-side signal exists, so 'nothing to write' and 'not running' look identical. ar-no-recent-write detects it without access to the job's own instrumentation. Threshold must be derived from the job's cadence, which is not knowable from this repo.

If that loop is missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged, eviction simply never runs. annotations.description: The cache is growing monotonically toward an OOM kill. This is the earliest actionable point in the memory chain and the reason to alert here rather than on memory: it gives hours to days of lead time, and it attributes the growth to the cache rather than to an unspecified leak. annotations.summary: p99 storage read latency is above 500ms
annotations.description: Every cache miss reads the entire backing file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size). This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after any restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been -- expect this to fire alongside KvstoreCrashLooping rather than independently of it. Measured at the storage boundary so the cost is attributed to the right layer instead of surfacing as unexplained end-to-end slowness. Set histogram buckets to span a small file through a degraded one; the prometheus_client defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate.

I am also restoring 'failure_mode_ids' on the two phase 4 probe entries in this same round, as I said I would if the probe came back negative -- leaving them on an unread key would make them strictly worse off than the other 19. No expression, threshold, severity, coverage status, exclusion reason, or analytical content changes anywhere.

annotations.summary: Cache entry count is large and still rising with no sign of eviction
annotations.description: The cache is growing monotonically toward an OOM kill. This is the earliest actionable point in the memory chain and the reason to alert here rather than on memory: it gives hours to days of lead time, and it attributes the growth to the cache rather than to an unspecified leak. The two conditions are both needed -- absolute size alone fires on a legitimately large working set, and positive derivative alone fires on ordinary warm-up. CALIBRATE the 500000 threshold against the container memory limit divided by average entry size before enabling; the value here is a placeholder, not a measurement. Growth is driven by the unique-key rate, not the request rate, so a scan or a crawler moves this far faster than traffic volume suggests.

annotations.summary: p99 storage read latency is above 500ms
annotations.description: Every cache miss reads the entire backing file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size). This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after any restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been -- expect this to fire alongside KvstoreCrashLooping rather than independently of it. Measured at the storage boundary so the cost is attributed to the right layer instead of surfacing as unexplained end-to-end slowness. Set histogram buckets to span a small file through a degraded one; the prometheus_client defaults are tuned for HTTP latencies and will saturate.

payload_or_id.title: Cache entry count and footprint grow without bound
payload_or_id.description: Entries are only ever added, never removed, so the dict grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys ever requested. Growth rate is set by the unique-key rate rather than the request rate, which means a scan, a crawler, or a key namespace with high cardinality drives it far faster than normal traffic would suggest. This is the observable precursor to the OOM kill and the point at which the chain can be caught with hours or days of warning instead of none.

payload_or_id.rationale: There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so slow reads produce no signal at all. ar-read-latency-high measures the user-facing symptom at the storage boundary; the miss-rate and file-size metrics explain it and are what make the alert actionable rather than merely true.

result.message: phase 3 coverage edit for 'fm-read-latency-degradation' touches the other side's field(s): alert_ids

event.text:
That error is the answer. "Touches the other side's field(s): `alert_ids`" — so `alert_ids` is a recognised linkage field, coverage must not carry it, and my phase 2 probe adding it to a **failure mode** was accepted without complaint. The linkage lives on the failure-mode entries, not on coverage.

Applying it to the remaining 23 non-excluded failure modes.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads a permanently stale value after a write
payload_or_id.description: get_value returns a value that was correct before the last write and is now wrong, and keeps returning it for the life of the process. Cache.get short-circuits on any resident key and never re-consults storage, so once a key is cached the only ways it can ever change are eviction or a restart. Neither happens: the write path does not invalidate, and the evictor's TTL check can never fire. The service reports outcome="success" for every one of these reads.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads None forever for a key that does exist in storage
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get caches the result of a miss, storing Entry(value=None) for keys absent from storage. If a key is read before the data-sync job writes it, the None is cached and served indefinitely afterwards -- the later write to storage cannot dislodge it. This is a distinct outcome from stale-value staleness because the key never had a correct cached value to go stale: a single premature read permanently hides a key from every client. Indistinguishable at the entrypoint from a legitimately absent key, since both return None with outcome="success".

payload_or_id.title: Process is OOM-killed, taking the service down
payload_or_id.description: The cache holds every key ever requested, so under sustained unique-key traffic resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed by the OOM killer or the container's memory limit. Every in-flight request fails and the service is unavailable until it restarts -- at which point the cache is empty and the climb begins again, giving a sawtooth of periodic outages whose interval depends only on traffic mix. Nothing in the process observes its own memory or entry count, so the first signal is the kill itself.

payload_or_id.title: get_value raises StorageError to the client
payload_or_id.description: A read that misses the cache reaches Storage.get, which converts any OSError into StorageError; api.py increments outcome="error" and re-raises to the caller. This is the one failure mode the service instruments today and the only one alertable without new instrumentation. Note the coupling to cache state: with a warm cache only miss traffic is affected, so a completely unreadable backing file can present as a partial rather than total failure, and its blast radius grows immediately after any restart.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads a corrupted or foreign value from delimiter collision
payload_or_id.description: The store's line format is unescaped "key,value" split on the first comma. A value containing a comma round-trips intact, but a key containing a comma is silently re-partitioned on read: writing key "a,b" with value "x" produces the line "a,b,x", which reads back as key "a" with value "b,x". A value containing a newline is worse -- it writes a spurious extra line that becomes a phantom key/value pair, and can shadow or overwrite a real key on the next put(). The result is a client receiving a well-formed value that belongs to a different key, reported as outcome="success". Silent data corruption with no signal at any layer.

payload_or_id.title: Previously written keys disappear from the store
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put rewrites the entire file from an in-memory dict via a single write_text, with no temp-file-and-rename and no lock. A crash, kill, or ENOSPC partway through leaves the file truncated or partially written, destroying keys that were never touched by the write that failed -- the blast radius of one bad write is the whole dataset. Clients see previously-good keys start returning None, or an unparseable tail. Recovery requires a restore; the service itself neither detects nor reports the loss. A lost or misconfigured file path presents identically, since Storage.get returns None rather than raising when the file is absent.

payload_or_id.title: Read latency degrades as the store file grows
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads the entire file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size) and the whole file is allocated per miss. This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after a restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been. There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so this manifests to clients as slow reads with no corresponding signal.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass evicts nothing due to a seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in epoch seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, which cache.py sets to `time.time() * 1000`. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS, so expired_keys is always empty and the pass always returns 0. The single mechanism that bounds cache memory and the single mechanism that eventually corrects a stale entry are the same mechanism, and it is dead. Rated critical despite not being user-visible because it is the shared root of both the OOM chain and the staleness chain, and it is the earliest point at which either can be detected.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass is a plain function; the scheduler loop that should call it periodically is sm-job-eviction-scheduler, which lives outside this repo. If that loop is missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged, eviction simply never runs. Attributed to the scheduler rather than to the pass because that is where the fault and the fix both sit -- a deployment problem, not a code problem -- mirroring how fm-data-sync-job-stopped is attributed to sm-job-data-sync rather than to the write path it drives. This is a separate failure from the unit mismatch in fm-evictor-never-evicts and produces identical downstream effects, which is what makes detection hard: a pass that returns 0 and a pass that never ran are indistinguishable unless the pass emits a signal on every execution. Fixing the unit bug alone leaves this failure entirely undetectable.

payload_or_id.title: Write path does not invalidate the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value takes a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put, never cache.evict(key). The seam needed to fix it already exists and is documented in cache.py as intended for exactly this caller. On its own this would bound staleness to one TTL period; combined with the dead evictor it makes staleness permanent. The unused parameter is the tell -- the invalidation was designed and then not wired.

payload_or_id.title: Cache stores negative results indefinitely
payload_or_id.description: On a storage miss, Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) rather than declining to cache. Two consequences: an attacker or a buggy client requesting random non-existent keys inflates the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain; and a key read before it is first written is permanently pinned to None. Negative caching is a legitimate design choice, but only with a TTL, and this cache has no working expiry. Kept as a metric gap rather than excluded because the share of cached entries holding None is a real, varying runtime quantity that distinguishes ordinary growth from miss-driven inflation.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file unreadable (permissions, I/O error, unmounted volume)
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get raises OSError -- and hence StorageError -- if the file exists but cannot be read: permission change, hardware or network-volume I/O error, unmounted path, or exhausted file descriptors. Note the asymmetry deliberately built into get(): a file that does not exist at all returns None rather than raising, so a lost or wrong path presents as every key having silently vanished rather than as an error. That variant is the more dangerous one, because it produces outcome="success" for every read and is covered instead by fm-storage-data-loss.

payload_or_id.title: Filesystem full or out of inodes on write
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put must materialise the entire dataset as a single string and write it in one call, so it needs free space of the order of the whole file on every single write, and briefly holds the dataset twice in memory. On ENOSPC the write_text fails partway, leaving the file truncated -- the non-atomic rewrite converts a full disk directly into dataset-wide data loss rather than into a rejected write.

payload_or_id.title: Reader observes the file mid-rewrite
payload_or_id.description: With no locking between get() and put(), a read overlapping a rewrite can see a truncated or partially written file. The read then returns None for keys that exist (they were in the not-yet-written tail) or raises StorageError on an I/O failure. Because misses are cached, a None read during this window is captured into the cache and outlives the rewrite that caused it -- a transient storage race is promoted into permanent wrong state.

payload_or_id.title: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: put() is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file. Two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish discards every key the first added. There is no lock, no compare-and-swap, and no version check, and both writers report success. Whether this can fire depends on the deployment -- a single-threaded sync job makes it unreachable -- so it warrants confirming the concurrency model rather than assuming either way.

payload_or_id.title: Unescaped delimiter format does not round-trip keys or values
payload_or_id.description: Keys and values are written raw with a comma separator and newline record terminator, with no escaping, quoting, or validation on either. Any key containing a comma, or any value containing a newline, produces a file that parses back into different data than was written. Nothing rejects such input at write time, so corruption is introduced silently and only surfaces on a later read.

payload_or_id.title: Store file grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows. Since every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites the whole file, cost per operation on both paths rises linearly with total keys ever written, and the non-atomic-rewrite risk window widens with it. Nothing measures or reports file size or key count.

payload_or_id.title: Metrics never reach a scrape endpoint, silently disabling all alerting
payload_or_id.description: The Counter is registered in api.py, but nothing in this repo starts an HTTP exposition server, calls start_http_server, or pushes to a gateway. If the surrounding deployment does not wire one up, the counter increments into a registry nobody reads. This is the failure mode that disables every other detection in this analysis: alert rules on absent series do not fire, so the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. Rated critical because its consequence is the silent loss of the entire alerting capability, and it must be verified rather than assumed before any phase 4 recommendation can be trusted.

payload_or_id.title: Write path emits no signal at all
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value increments no counter, records no latency, and logs nothing on success or failure. Write volume, write errors, and the time since the last successful write are all unobservable, so a write path that has stopped entirely looks exactly like one with nothing to do. Every staleness and data-loss chain in this document originates here and is undetectable at its origin.

payload_or_id.title: StorageError on write is neither caught nor recorded by the service
payload_or_id.description: update_value lets StorageError propagate to its caller with no counter, no log, and no re-raise wrapping. Whether that failure is ever noticed depends entirely on the out-of-repo sync job's own error handling; if it swallows or retries silently, writes can fail indefinitely while the service serves increasingly outdated data and reports every read as a success.

payload_or_id.title: Cache emits no hit, miss, size, or eviction signal
payload_or_id.description: Cache exposes no metrics of any kind. Entry count, hit/miss ratio, and read-through rate are all invisible, which is what makes the unbounded-growth chain undetectable before the OOM kill and makes it impossible to tell whether a stable error rate reflects a healthy backend or merely a cache warm enough that reads never reach it.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass discards the one number it computes
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass returns the count of evicted keys with a docstring stating the purpose is so a caller can observe progress, but nothing records it -- no counter, no log, no last-run timestamp. The result is that both evictor failure modes are silent: a broken pass returning 0 forever and a pass that stopped being scheduled produce byte-identical evidence, namely none.

payload_or_id.title: Upstream data-sync job stops writing
payload_or_id.description: The periodic job that drives update_value is the only writer. If it stops, crashes, or is descheduled, storage quietly freezes at its last state and the whole system serves indefinitely old data while every component reports healthy. The job is out of repo, so the only place its liveness could be inferred from inside the service is a write-side signal, which does not exist -- see fm-write-path-uninstrumented.

The two-entry probe was decisive: both probe alerts moved from linkage_inconsistency to empty_linkage_alert_recommendation, proving unread keys report empty_linkage and read keys report inconsistency -- so 'failure_mode_ids' on the alert side was correct all along and the defect was never a field name. The reciprocal probe then produced the actual answer as a rejection message: 'phase 3 coverage edit for fm-read-latency-degradation touches the other side's field(s): alert_ids'. That names the field ('alert_ids'), establishes that coverage must not carry it, and -- because the identical key was accepted without complaint on the phase 2 failure-mode entry in the same round -- locates it on failure-modes. The linkage is two-sided between failure modes and alerts: the alert declares failure_mode_ids, the failure mode declares alert_ids, and coverage declares neither. FIX APPLIED: all 24 non-excluded failure modes now carry alert_ids naming the alert or alerts that detect them, the exact inverse of the alert-side failure_mode_ids, verified in both directions. The 4 excluded modes were deliberately left without alert_ids, preserving their zero coverage. The two phase 4 probe entries were restored to failure_mode_ids as promised, with expressions, thresholds, severities and annotations byte-identical to their approved versions. event.text:
Found it — and by experiment, not inference.

**The two probes settled the name question.** Both flipped from `linkage_inconsistency` to `empty_linkage_alert_recommendation`, which establishes the diagnostic's grammar: *unread* keys report `empty_linkage`, *read* keys report `inconsistency`. So `failure_mode_ids` on the alert side was correct from the start. The defect was never a field name — four rounds of renaming were chasing the wrong thing.

**The reciprocal probe then gave the answer in a rejection message:** `phase 3 coverage edit ... touches the other side's field(s): alert_ids`. That single line names the field, says coverage must not hold it, and — because the identical key was silently *accepted* on the phase 2 failure-mode entry in the very same round — locates where it belongs.

**The model is two-sided between failure modes and alerts:**

- alert declares `failure_mode_ids`
- failure mode declares `alert_ids`
- coverage declares **neither**

That's why coverage-side reciprocity never helped: I was completing the relationship on an artifact that isn't party to it.

**Fix applied:** all 24 non-excluded failure modes now carry `alert_ids`, the exact inverse of the alert-side linkage, checked in both directions. The 4 excluded modes deliberately have none. Both probe alerts are restored to `failure_mode_ids` with expressions, thresholds, severities and annotations byte-identical to their approved versions. Full payloads throughout, so every description, severity, `coverage_status`, component and `caused_by` chain survives the replace semantics — including the earlier repointing of `fm-evictor-not-scheduled` to `sm-job-eviction-scheduler`.

**One residual:** the 24 coverage entries still carry the `alerts` key from an earlier repair. It's dead metadata rather than harmful — `linkage_inconsistency` predates it — but it sits on the wrong side of the relationship and should be stripped if phase 3 opens again.

The lesson worth recording: the bounded two-entry probe cost one round and produced a definitive answer, after four full-artifact rewrites produced none. I should have run it four rounds earlier, the first time a rename failed.
The amendment now also covers phase 2, phase 3 (pulled in by reference to your changes). Propose repairs via propose_edits, then call run_control with amend_complete when done.

Phase 3 is in scope, which is exactly the condition I flagged for the outstanding cleanup: the 24 coverage entries still carry the `alerts` key from an earlier repair. Now that the linkage model is known — alert declares `failure_mode_ids`, failure mode declares `alert_ids`, coverage declares neither — that key is dead metadata sitting on the wrong side of the relationship. Stripping it.

payload_or_id.rationale: kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} increments on exactly this failure; only an alert rule is missing. Caveat: because cache hits never reach storage, this counter under-reports a storage outage in proportion to cache warmth, so the rule triggers on error ratio against total requests rather than absolute rate.

Every OSError on read becomes a StorageError and is already counted as outcome="error", so this is detectable today with a rule alone. Limit of that coverage: it catches the file being present but unreadable, not the file being absent, because Storage.get returns None rather than raising -- that variant is covered under fm-storage-data-loss.

The existing counter reports outcome="success" for every stale read, so no rule over current instrumentation can detect this at any threshold. Detection moves upstream to the age of the oldest cached entry and to writer-sourced invalidations. Neither observes staleness directly -- that would require comparing cached against stored values -- but together they detect both mechanisms that produce it.

Today a poisoned None and a legitimately absent key are byte-identical at the only instrumented point. The found label makes the user-visible symptom detectable; the negative-entries gauge sizes the at-risk population. Full certainty still requires correlating a found=false read against a key present in storage, which no single metric can express.

Nothing observes memory or entry count, so the first evidence today is the kill itself. Process memory is the late backstop and restart count confirms the sawtooth after the fact; the precursor worth acting on is cache entry count, which gives hours to days of lead time.

Corrupted values are well-formed strings returned as outcome="success"; no metric can detect that a returned value belongs to a different key. Covered by prevention plus a proof-of-guard counter rather than by detection: the counter requires write-time validation, which converts silent corruption into a loud rejection. Stated plainly because this is the one failure mode where instrumentation alone is not a sufficient answer.

Vanished keys return None with outcome="success", indistinguishable from keys that never existed. Stored key count is the only proposal capable of detecting it: the store has no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and any drop is by definition data loss.

There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so slow reads produce no signal at all. The duration histogram measures the user-facing symptom at the storage boundary; miss rate and file size explain it and are what make the alert actionable rather than merely true.

The evictor emits nothing, so a pass that removes zero entries forever is silent. Evicted-key count costs nothing to add because run_eviction_pass already computes and discards the number. Oldest-entry age is the stronger signal: it asserts the invariant the evictor exists to maintain, so it survives the fix and catches any future regression that leaves eviction running but ineffective.

Not detectable today, and specifically not separable from fm-evictor-never-evicts. A last-completion timestamp resolves that: it keeps producing a rising, alertable value when the pass stops entirely, which a rate() over a counter does not. The two failure modes need different fixes -- a code change versus a deployment fix -- which is why distinguishing them is worth a dedicated metric.

The write path emits nothing, so the missing invalidation is invisible until a user reads stale data. Together these make the defect itself machine-checkable: writes occurring while writer-sourced invalidations remain at zero states the bug directly, and guards against the fix being dropped in a later refactor.

No metric observes cache size. Entry count covers this directly and is the highest-value single addition in the analysis, since this failure mode is the sole cause of the OOM outage and gives long lead time. The negative-entry gauge separates miss-driven inflation from legitimate working-set growth, which call for different remedies.

Not observable today. Kept as a gap rather than an exclusion because, unlike the missing size bound, the count of resident None entries is a genuinely varying runtime quantity: it distinguishes an adversarial or buggy key-space probe from ordinary growth, and sizes the population at risk of permanent None-pinning.

Write-side OSError is entirely uninstrumented today, so a full disk is silent until it has already truncated the dataset. The operations counter catches the failed write; free-space catches it before it happens. Headroom needed is roughly one whole file size, because put() rewrites the entire store -- a generic percentage-based disk alert may fire too late.

A torn read surfaces either as a StorageError, already counted at the entrypoint though not attributed to this cause, or as a silent None that gets cached and outlives the race. The silent variant remains undetected -- a residual gap worth stating rather than papering over.

OPEN QUESTION, carried from phase 2 and still unresolved by the code: whether concurrent writers exist depends on the out-of-repo sync job's threading model. If it is single-threaded and the only writer, this mode is unreachable and should be reclassified as excluded. The recommendation is explicitly conditional and also requires adding the conflict detection it counts -- the metric cannot be built on its own.

Nothing validates keys or values on write, so malformed records enter the store silently and only surface as corruption on a later read. The counter requires that validation to be added first; it then proves the guard is holding and sizes any pre-existing damage found while reading.

Neither file size nor key count is measured. Both come at no extra I/O cost since the values are already in hand at the end of Storage.put. Growth here compounds two other chains -- read latency and the non-atomic-rewrite risk window -- so it warrants a slow-burn warning rather than being left to the latency alert alone.

Self-referential and therefore worth stating carefully: this cannot be detected by any metric this service emits, because its whole content is that emitted metrics do not arrive. Detection must come from the monitoring system's own view -- Prometheus target UP, or an absent() rule over a series known to be always present. It is a prerequisite for every other item in this phase, and its verification step is manual by necessity.

This failure mode is the absence of instrumentation itself, so it is a gap by definition. Both recommendations sit in Storage rather than in admin.py deliberately: instrumenting the datastore boundary cannot be bypassed by a future second writer, whereas instrumenting the one known caller can.

StorageError from put() propagates into out-of-repo code with no counter, log, or trace inside the service. An error-labeled put counter makes write failures visible from inside this service, which matters because whether the sync job reports its own errors is outside this codebase's control and cannot be assumed.

The cache emits nothing at all. Beyond enabling the growth and staleness chains, the hit/miss counter fixes a subtle blind spot in the metric that does exist: a flat error rate cannot currently distinguish a healthy backend from a cache warm enough that storage is never exercised, meaning storage could be entirely broken while the service looks fine.

The pass computes the eviction count expressly so a caller can observe progress, per its own docstring, and then nothing records it. Recording it plus a completion timestamp is the minimum that makes the evictor's two failure modes distinguishable from each other and from healthy operation.

A frozen upstream job is invisible from inside the service today: no write-side signal exists, so 'nothing to write' and 'not running' look identical. A last-successful-write timestamp detects it without needing access to the job's own instrumentation. Threshold must be derived from the job's expected cadence, which is not knowable from this repo.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_entries
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of current cache entry count
payload_or_id.description: Number of entries currently resident in Cache._entries.
payload_or_id.details: Set the gauge to len(self._entries) after each insertion in Cache.get and each removal in Cache.evict, or register it as a callback gauge so the value is computed at scrape time (cheaper and impossible to drift from reality). This is the single highest-value new metric in the analysis: it converts the OOM chain from undetectable-until-the-kill into a trend with hours or days of lead time, and because the count only ever rises while eviction is broken, a monotonic climb across a scrape window is direct evidence that no eviction is happening regardless of which of the two evictor faults is responsible.
payload_or_id.rationale: Detects the precursor rather than the outage. Memory-based detection alone would fire far later and would not distinguish cache growth from any other leak.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_get_value_requests_total
payload_or_id.title: kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}
payload_or_id.definition_site: kvstore/api.py:19-23 (Counter declaration); incremented at kvstore/api.py:30 with outcome="error" and kvstore/api.py:32 with outcome="success"
payload_or_id.description: The only metric implemented anywhere in this codebase. Counts calls to get_value, labeled outcome=success|error. It is incremented once per call on both paths, so it doubles as a request-rate signal. Its reach is strictly limited by where it sits: it observes the return of Cache.get and cannot see whether that return came from the cache or from storage, nor whether the value is current. Cache hits, misses, storage latency, storage errors on the write path, evictions, and entry counts are all invisible to it. The outcome="error" label is driven solely by StorageError raised out of a read that reached storage.
payload_or_id.notes: The Counter is registered against the prometheus_client default registry, but no exposition path exists in this repo -- no start_http_server, no make_wsgi_app, no generate_latest, no /metrics handler (verified by grep across all source files). Whether this series reaches Prometheus at all depends entirely on out-of-repo deployment wiring.
