payload_or_id.rationale: The existing counter reports outcome="success" for every stale read, so no rule over current instrumentation can detect this at any threshold. Detection moves upstream to the age of the oldest cached entry and to writer-sourced invalidations.

A poisoned None and a legitimately absent key are byte-identical at the only instrumented point today. The found label makes the user-visible symptom detectable; the negative-entries gauge sizes the at-risk population.

Nothing observes memory or entry count, so the first evidence today is the kill itself. Memory is the late backstop and restart count confirms the sawtooth; the precursor worth acting on is cache entry count.

kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome="error"} increments on exactly this failure; only the alert rule is missing. Expressed as a ratio because cache hits never reach storage, so an absolute rate is calibrated to traffic that may not be reaching storage at all.

Corrupted values are well-formed strings returned as outcome="success"; no metric can detect that a returned value belongs to a different key. Covered by prevention plus a proof-of-guard counter rather than by detection.

Vanished keys return None with outcome="success". Stored key count is the only proposal capable of detecting it: the store has no delete, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing and any drop is by definition data loss.
There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service. The duration histogram measures the user-facing symptom at the storage boundary; miss rate and file size explain it.
The evictor emits nothing. Evicted-key count costs nothing to add since the pass already computes and discards it; oldest-entry age asserts the invariant and survives the fix as a regression guard.
Not detectable today and not separable from fm-evictor-never-evicts. A last-completion timestamp keeps producing a rising alertable value when the pass stops entirely, which a rate() rule does not.
The write path emits nothing, so the missing invalidation is invisible until a user reads stale data. Writes occurring while writer-sourced invalidations remain zero states the bug directly.

No metric observes cache size. Entry count covers this directly and is the highest-value single addition in the analysis, since this failure mode is the sole cause of the OOM outage and gives long lead time.

Not observable today. Kept as a gap rather than an exclusion because the count of resident None entries is a genuinely varying runtime quantity that distinguishes a key-space probe from ordinary growth.

Every OSError on read becomes a StorageError and is already counted. It catches the file being present but unreadable, not absent -- Storage.get returns None rather than raising, and that variant is covered under fm-storage-data-loss.
Write-side OSError is entirely uninstrumented, so a full disk is silent until it has truncated the dataset. Headroom needed is roughly one whole file size because put() rewrites the entire store.
A torn read surfaces either as a StorageError, which the storage read-error alert catches, or as a silent None that gets cached and outlives the race. The silent variant remains a residual gap.

OPEN QUESTION: whether concurrent writers exist depends on the out-of-repo sync job's threading model. If single-threaded, this mode is unreachable and should be reclassified as excluded, dropping the conditional alert and its metric.
Nothing validates keys or values on write, so malformed records enter the store silently and surface as corruption on a later read. The counter requires that validation to be added first.
Neither file size nor key count is measured, and both come at no extra I/O cost since the values are already in hand at the end of Storage.put. Alerted on trajectory rather than current value.

Self-referential: cannot be detected by any metric this service emits, because its content is that emitted metrics do not arrive. Detection comes from the monitoring system's own target view. Prerequisite for every other alert in the run.

This failure mode is the absence of instrumentation itself. Both recommendations sit in Storage rather than admin.py so they cannot be bypassed by a future second writer; the absent() alert detects a regression back to the uninstrumented state.

StorageError from put() propagates into out-of-repo code with no counter or log. An error-labeled put counter makes write failures visible from inside this service, since the sync job's own error handling is outside this codebase's control.

The cache emits nothing at all. The hit/miss counter also fixes a blind spot in the existing metric: a flat error rate cannot distinguish a healthy backend from a cache warm enough that storage is never exercised.

The pass computes the eviction count expressly so a caller can observe progress, per its own docstring, and nothing records it. Recording it plus a completion timestamp makes the evictor's two failure modes distinguishable.

A frozen upstream job is invisible from inside the service: no write-side signal exists, so 'nothing to write' and 'not running' look identical. Threshold must come from the job's cadence, which is not knowable from this repo.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_entries
payload_or_id.title: Gauge of current cache entry count
payload_or_id.description: Number of entries currently resident in Cache._entries.
payload_or_id.details: Set the gauge to len(self._entries) after each insertion in Cache.get and each removal in Cache.evict, or register it as a callback gauge so the value is computed at scrape time (cheaper and impossible to drift from reality). This is the single highest-value new metric in the analysis: it converts the OOM chain from undetectable-until-the-kill into a trend with hours or days of lead time, and because the count only ever rises while eviction is broken, a monotonic climb across a scrape window is direct evidence that no eviction is happening regardless of which of the two evictor faults is responsible.
payload_or_id.rationale: Detects the precursor rather than the outage. Memory-based detection alone would fire far later and would not distinguish cache growth from any other leak.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_get_value_requests_total
payload_or_id.title: kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}
payload_or_id.definition_site: kvstore/api.py:19-23 (Counter declaration); incremented at kvstore/api.py:30 with outcome="error" and kvstore/api.py:32 with outcome="success"
payload_or_id.description: The only metric implemented anywhere in this codebase. Counts calls to get_value, labeled outcome=success|error. It is incremented once per call on both paths, so it doubles as a request-rate signal. Its reach is strictly limited by where it sits: it observes the return of Cache.get and cannot see whether that return came from the cache or from storage, nor whether the value is current. Cache hits, misses, storage latency, storage errors on the write path, evictions, and entry counts are all invisible to it. The outcome="error" label is driven solely by StorageError raised out of a read that reached storage.
payload_or_id.notes: The Counter is registered against the prometheus_client default registry, but no exposition path exists in this repo -- no start_http_server, no make_wsgi_app, no generate_latest, no /metrics handler (verified by grep across all source files). Whether this series reaches Prometheus at all depends entirely on out-of-repo deployment wiring.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads a permanently stale value after a write
payload_or_id.description: get_value returns a value that was correct before the last write and is now wrong, and keeps returning it for the life of the process. Cache.get short-circuits on any resident key and never re-consults storage, so once a key is cached the only ways it can ever change are eviction or a restart. Neither happens: the write path does not invalidate, and the evictor's TTL check can never fire. The service reports outcome="success" for every one of these reads.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads None forever for a key that does exist in storage
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get caches the result of a miss, storing Entry(value=None) for keys absent from storage. If a key is read before the data-sync job writes it, the None is cached and served indefinitely afterwards -- the later write to storage cannot dislodge it. This is a distinct outcome from stale-value staleness because the key never had a correct cached value to go stale: a single premature read permanently hides a key from every client. Indistinguishable at the entrypoint from a legitimately absent key, since both return None with outcome="success".

payload_or_id.title: Process is OOM-killed, taking the service down
payload_or_id.description: The cache holds every key ever requested, so under sustained unique-key traffic resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed by the OOM killer or the container's memory limit. Every in-flight request fails and the service is unavailable until it restarts -- at which point the cache is empty and the climb begins again, giving a sawtooth of periodic outages whose interval depends only on traffic mix. Nothing in the process observes its own memory or entry count, so the first signal is the kill itself.

payload_or_id.title: get_value raises StorageError to the client
payload_or_id.description: A read that misses the cache reaches Storage.get, which converts any OSError into StorageError; api.py increments outcome="error" and re-raises to the caller. This is the one failure mode the service instruments today and the only one alertable without new instrumentation. Note the coupling to cache state: with a warm cache only miss traffic is affected, so a completely unreadable backing file can present as a partial rather than total failure, and its blast radius grows immediately after any restart.

payload_or_id.title: Client reads a corrupted or foreign value from delimiter collision
payload_or_id.description: The store's line format is unescaped "key,value" split on the first comma. A value containing a comma round-trips intact, but a key containing a comma is silently re-partitioned on read: writing key "a,b" with value "x" produces the line "a,b,x", which reads back as key "a" with value "b,x". A value containing a newline is worse -- it writes a spurious extra line that becomes a phantom key/value pair, and can shadow or overwrite a real key on the next put(). The result is a client receiving a well-formed value that belongs to a different key, reported as outcome="success". Silent data corruption with no signal at any layer.

payload_or_id.title: Previously written keys disappear from the store
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put rewrites the entire file from an in-memory dict via a single write_text, with no temp-file-and-rename and no lock. A crash, kill, or ENOSPC partway through leaves the file truncated or partially written, destroying keys that were never touched by the write that failed -- the blast radius of one bad write is the whole dataset. Clients see previously-good keys start returning None, or an unparseable tail. Recovery requires a restore; the service itself neither detects nor reports the loss. A lost or misconfigured file path presents identically, since Storage.get returns None rather than raising when the file is absent.

payload_or_id.title: Read latency degrades as the store file grows
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads the entire file into memory and scans it line by line, so miss latency is O(file size) and the whole file is allocated per miss. This is invisible while the cache is warm and becomes the dominant cost immediately after a restart, when every request is a miss against the largest the file has ever been. There is no latency instrumentation anywhere in the service, so this manifests to clients as slow reads with no corresponding signal.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass evicts nothing due to a seconds/milliseconds unit mismatch
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in epoch seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, which cache.py sets to `time.time() * 1000`. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS, so expired_keys is always empty and the pass always returns 0. The single mechanism that bounds cache memory and the single mechanism that eventually corrects a stale entry are the same mechanism, and it is dead. Rated critical despite not being user-visible because it is the shared root of both the OOM chain and the staleness chain, and it is the earliest point at which either can be detected.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass is a plain function; the scheduler loop that should call it periodically is sm-job-eviction-scheduler, which lives outside this repo. If that loop is missing, misconfigured, crashed, or wedged, eviction simply never runs. Attributed to the scheduler rather than to the pass because that is where the fault and the fix both sit -- a deployment problem, not a code problem -- mirroring how fm-data-sync-job-stopped is attributed to sm-job-data-sync rather than to the write path it drives. This is a separate failure from the unit mismatch in fm-evictor-never-evicts and produces identical downstream effects, which is what makes detection hard: a pass that returns 0 and a pass that never ran are indistinguishable unless the pass emits a signal on every execution. Fixing the unit bug alone leaves this failure entirely undetectable.

payload_or_id.title: Write path does not invalidate the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value takes a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put, never cache.evict(key). The seam needed to fix it already exists and is documented in cache.py as intended for exactly this caller. On its own this would bound staleness to one TTL period; combined with the dead evictor it makes staleness permanent. The unused parameter is the tell -- the invalidation was designed and then not wired.

payload_or_id.title: Cache entry count and footprint grow without bound
payload_or_id.description: Entries are only ever added, never removed, so the dict grows monotonically with the number of distinct keys ever requested. Growth rate is set by the unique-key rate rather than the request rate, which means a scan, a crawler, or a key namespace with high cardinality drives it far faster than normal traffic would suggest. This is the observable precursor to the OOM kill and the point at which the chain can be caught with hours or days of warning instead of none.

payload_or_id.title: Cache stores negative results indefinitely
payload_or_id.description: On a storage miss, Cache.get stores Entry(value=None) rather than declining to cache. Two consequences: an attacker or a buggy client requesting random non-existent keys inflates the cache at will with no storage-side cost, accelerating the OOM chain; and a key read before it is first written is permanently pinned to None. Negative caching is a legitimate design choice, but only with a TTL, and this cache has no working expiry. Kept as a metric gap rather than excluded because the share of cached entries holding None is a real, varying runtime quantity that distinguishes ordinary growth from miss-driven inflation.

payload_or_id.title: Backing file unreadable (permissions, I/O error, unmounted volume)
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get raises OSError -- and hence StorageError -- if the file exists but cannot be read: permission change, hardware or network-volume I/O error, unmounted path, or exhausted file descriptors. Note the asymmetry deliberately built into get(): a file that does not exist at all returns None rather than raising, so a lost or wrong path presents as every key having silently vanished rather than as an error. That variant is the more dangerous one, because it produces outcome="success" for every read and is covered instead by fm-storage-data-loss.

payload_or_id.title: Filesystem full or out of inodes on write
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put must materialise the entire dataset as a single string and write it in one call, so it needs free space of the order of the whole file on every single write, and briefly holds the dataset twice in memory. On ENOSPC the write_text fails partway, leaving the file truncated -- the non-atomic rewrite converts a full disk directly into dataset-wide data loss rather than into a rejected write.

payload_or_id.title: Reader observes the file mid-rewrite
payload_or_id.description: With no locking between get() and put(), a read overlapping a rewrite can see a truncated or partially written file. The read then returns None for keys that exist (they were in the not-yet-written tail) or raises StorageError on an I/O failure. Because misses are cached, a None read during this window is captured into the cache and outlives the rewrite that caused it -- a transient storage race is promoted into permanent wrong state.

payload_or_id.title: Concurrent writes silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: put() is an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the entire file. Two writers interleaving each read the same prior state and each write back their own full copy, so the second to finish discards every key the first added. There is no lock, no compare-and-swap, and no version check, and both writers report success. Whether this can fire depends on the deployment -- a single-threaded sync job makes it unreachable -- so it warrants confirming the concurrency model rather than assuming either way.

payload_or_id.title: Unescaped delimiter format does not round-trip keys or values
payload_or_id.description: Keys and values are written raw with a comma separator and newline record terminator, with no escaping, quoting, or validation on either. Any key containing a comma, or any value containing a newline, produces a file that parses back into different data than was written. Nothing rejects such input at write time, so corruption is introduced silently and only surfaces on a later read.

payload_or_id.title: Store file grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: put() has no delete, expiry, or compaction, so the file only ever grows. Since every read scans the whole file and every write reads and rewrites the whole file, cost per operation on both paths rises linearly with total keys ever written, and the non-atomic-rewrite risk window widens with it. Nothing measures or reports file size or key count.

payload_or_id.title: Metrics never reach a scrape endpoint, silently disabling all alerting
payload_or_id.description: The Counter is registered in api.py, but nothing in this repo starts an HTTP exposition server, calls start_http_server, or pushes to a gateway. If the surrounding deployment does not wire one up, the counter increments into a registry nobody reads. This is the failure mode that disables every other detection in this analysis: alert rules on absent series do not fire, so the monitoring system reports all-clear precisely when it is blind. Rated critical because its consequence is the silent loss of the entire alerting capability, and it must be verified rather than assumed before any phase 4 recommendation can be trusted.

payload_or_id.title: Write path emits no signal at all
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value increments no counter, records no latency, and logs nothing on success or failure. Write volume, write errors, and the time since the last successful write are all unobservable, so a write path that has stopped entirely looks exactly like one with nothing to do. Every staleness and data-loss chain in this document originates here and is undetectable at its origin.

payload_or_id.title: StorageError on write is neither caught nor recorded by the service
payload_or_id.description: update_value lets StorageError propagate to its caller with no counter, no log, and no re-raise wrapping. Whether that failure is ever noticed depends entirely on the out-of-repo sync job's own error handling; if it swallows or retries silently, writes can fail indefinitely while the service serves increasingly outdated data and reports every read as a success.

payload_or_id.title: Cache emits no hit, miss, size, or eviction signal
payload_or_id.description: Cache exposes no metrics of any kind. Entry count, hit/miss ratio, and read-through rate are all invisible, which is what makes the unbounded-growth chain undetectable before the OOM kill and makes it impossible to tell whether a stable error rate reflects a healthy backend or merely a cache warm enough that reads never reach it.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass discards the one number it computes
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass returns the count of evicted keys with a docstring stating the purpose is so a caller can observe progress, but nothing records it -- no counter, no log, no last-run timestamp. The result is that both evictor failure modes are silent: a broken pass returning 0 forever and a pass that stopped being scheduled produce byte-identical evidence, namely none.

payload_or_id.title: Upstream data-sync job stops writing
payload_or_id.description: The periodic job that drives update_value is the only writer. If it stops, crashes, or is descheduled, storage quietly freezes at its last state and the whole system serves indefinitely old data while every component reports healthy. The job is out of repo, so the only place its liveness could be inferred from inside the service is a write-side signal, which does not exist -- see fm-write-path-uninstrumented.

payload.summary: Residual cleanup, now actionable because phases 2 and 3 came into scope. Removed dead alert_ids metadata from two places where I had added it under theories the probes disproved: the 24 failure-mode entries in phase 2 (added on the two-sided failure-mode/alert theory) and the two phase 3 probe entries mr-cache-entries and mx-get-value-requests-total (added to test whether the metric layer owned the field). Now that the real rule is known -- a failure mode counts as mapped only when its own coverage entry's alert_ids lists the covering alert, proposed under phase 4 -- those copies were duplicate assertions of a relationship the schema locates on coverage, and duplicate linkage that nothing reads is exactly the kind of thing a later reader treats as authoritative. All removals were done by full-payload update with every other field byte-identical to the approved state: titles, severities, user_visible flags, coverage_status values, components (including fm-evictor-not-scheduled's attribution to sm-job-eviction-scheduler), descriptions and caused_by chains on the failure modes; name, type, labels, definition_site, description, exposed and notes on the metric; kind, type, component, failure_mode_ids, description, details and rationale on the recommendation. The 4 excluded failure modes were not touched, as they never carried alert_ids. Phase 4 is unchanged from the previous round: 21 alerts carrying failure_mode_ids and metric_ids, and 24 coverage entries carrying alert_ids, which is the linkage that actually counts. IF REMOVING failure-modes alert_ids TURNS OUT TO BE WRONG -- that is, if a new defect appears naming those entries -- it is a one-round restore, since the mapping is unchanged and recorded in the coverage entries. I judged removal the better risk because the evidence is that the field was accepted but never read there: adding it to all 24 did not change the unmapped verdict for any of them. No analytical content changed anywhere in this repair: 9 components, 28 failure modes (24 alert-mapped, 4 reasoned exclusions), 1 implemented metric, 17 metric recommendations, 21 PromQL alert rules.

event.text:
Residual cleanup done, now that phases 2 and 3 were in scope.

**Removed dead `alert_ids` from two places I'd added it under disproved theories:**

- The 24 **failure-mode** entries (added on the two-sided failure-mode↔alert theory)
- The two phase 3 **probe** entries, `mr-cache-entries` and `mx-get-value-requests-total` (added to test whether the metric layer owned the field)

With the real rule now known — a failure mode counts as mapped only when its own **coverage** entry's `alert_ids` lists the alert, proposed under **phase 4** — those copies were duplicate assertions of a relationship the schema locates elsewhere. Duplicate linkage that nothing reads is precisely what a later reader mistakes for authoritative.

Every removal was a full-payload update with all other fields byte-identical to the approved state — including `fm-evictor-not-scheduled`'s attribution to `sm-job-eviction-scheduler`, all `caused_by` chains, and the metric's `definition_site` and exposure note. The 4 excluded failure modes were untouched; they never carried the field.

**One judgement call worth flagging:** removing `alert_ids` from failure modes is a bet that the field was accepted-but-never-read there. The evidence supports it — adding it to all 24 changed no verdict — but if a defect appears naming those entries, restoring is a single round, since the mapping itself is unchanged and lives in the coverage entries.

**Final state:** 9 components, 28 failure modes (24 alert-mapped via coverage `alert_ids`, 4 reasoned exclusions), 1 implemented metric, 17 metric recommendations, 21 PromQL alert rules — no analytical content altered by any repair round.
The amendment was approved; its changes are now part of the run.

Approved. The run is complete and the artifacts are now clean.

**Final state**

| | |
|---|---|
| Components | 9 |
| Failure modes | 28 — 24 alert-mapped, 4 reasoned exclusions |
| Metrics | 1 implemented, 17 recommended |
| Alerts | 21 PromQL rules |

Linkage resolved: alerts declare `failure_mode_ids`, coverage entries declare `alert_ids` (proposed under phase 4), and no duplicate copies remain on the failure-mode or metric artifacts.

**For the service, in order:**

1. Verify `/metrics` is genuinely exposed and scraped — by hand. Everything else rests on it, and its failure mode is silence rather than error.
2. Add `kvstore_cache_entries` → `kvstore_storage_operations_total` → `kvstore_storage_keys`.
3. Fix the seconds/milliseconds comparison in `evictor.py` — one bug that is simultaneously the only bound on cache memory and the only mechanism that would ever correct a stale entry.
4. Settle the writer concurrency model; replace the five CALIBRATE thresholds.

Expect `KvstoreWritesNotInvalidatingCache` to fire immediately against current code — that's the missing `cache.evict` call stated as an alert, and it should go quiet by fixing the code, not the rule.

**One lesson worth carrying forward.** The linkage cost far more rounds than it should have, and the decisive error was mine: when the coverage edit was rejected as *"touches the other side's field: `alert_ids`,"* I read "other side" as *wrong artifact* and never considered *wrong phase*. Both the field name and the artifact were correct on that first attempt. The probes that followed were sound and their conclusions held — but they varied field names and artifacts while holding the phase tag fixed, because I'd assumed the phase followed from the artifact rather than from which side of a cross-phase relationship a field belongs to. An assumption you don't know you're making is invisible to elimination testing, which is why four careful rounds still converged on nothing.
